SQLite store, rules with hoisting, the meter, the interpreter, the partition
log, at-most-once, the day-two classifier, wire forms), `snapback4-lang`
(Quarry lexer, parser, binder, diagnostics, the TypeScript emitter),
`snapback4` (verbs and the HTTP wire), `snapback4-sim` (the deterministic
world hosting the engine and a replica device), `snapback4-difftest` (seeded
Quarry source generator, rewrite and meter oracles, optional Postgres store
oracles with prefetch on/off, the server-against-device oracle on both device stores, the engine-against-Lean-model oracle, structural shrinking and replay; not published or linked by shipped crates), `snapback4-device` (the
interpreter over a `DeviceStore`: the core's SQLite under the native
module for Expo and Exact2 hosts, memory under wasm on the web; one

the language card and the keyword cards; packages: `snapback4` (the client
over the device and the CLI shim), `snapback4-darwin-arm64` and `snapback4-linux-x64` (the binaries), `snapback4-expo`

Quarry store testing (LLP 3000.035 §5.1): `SNAPBACK4_EVAL_POSTGRES` is an
explicit evaluation connection. The factory owns one physical schema per worker,
restores its rows and bookkeeping, installs the compiled fixture, then opens the
ordinary engine. Mutation attempts restore a seeded snapshot; shrinking reuses
that same factory. `Database::connect_fresh()` is an opt-in test mode. Fresh and
restored outcomes must serialize to identical bytes. The local wire observer
retains SQLSTATE, message, detail and SQL statement before the public query API
converts a driver error to a refusal; it never changes the traffic.

Reads sweep every public boundary. Mutations compare every discovered position
twice on SQLite, and compare up to eight seeded positions per dimension on
Postgres (including first/last), plus the case's original budget. Sampling
counters are in `store_stats`; each selected position runs prefetch on and off.
Physical prefetch counters are separate from the exact public outcome record.
The widened generator (`src/widen.rs`) emits prefetch-reachable reads: pages
projecting `tags[.tag]` and `tags[name = .label]` (a `Get` and a unique
`Lookup` whose keys vary across rows) and a loop reading `tags[row.tag]`, so
`store_stats` reports marked reads, transferred rows, cases with a transfer
and `prefetch_consumption_witness_probes` (fewer database calls with prefetch
on: cached answers were consumed). A planted cached-hit-to-miss fault is caught
by the random corpus (LLP 3000.035 §5.1; the closed
[coverage ticket](../issues/closed/20261007-quarry-store-oracle-prefetch-coverage-gap.md)).
Heap is charged identically on every store and the device (LLP 3000.007
§20.24.5); any disagreement is a ticket candidate, never normalized into a pass.
The cluster regression asserts it finds no signature and refuses any new one.

`run-stores --seconds N` stops each worker between cases after N seconds; a case
and any shrinking already underway finish. `cases` remains the requested count,
`generated` is actual completed generation, and `time_limited_workers` reports
the early stop. Slowest-case timing includes generation, comparisons, shrinking
and artifact saving. It does not silently claim the requested million. The scheduled
runner rejects incomplete reports; its own `--hours` option instead chooses a
case count from a 256-case calibration of both campaigns, with 20% headroom and
a million-case cap. This is a sizing estimate, not a hard deadline.

Generator widening (`src/widen.rs`, LLP 3000.035 §5.1): from a stream
independent of the base generator (`generate::base`; a seed it leaves alone is
the base case byte for byte), cases gain prefetch-reachable reads, mutation
blocks (lets, `require`, `if`, several writes to `key` and `k2`, reads after
writes), a prelude of mutations `prep0..` run in order on the same store before
`run` (`Case::steps`, sometimes as the other viewer; `observe` then reads both
keys), and expiry (`expire at .until`, a clock advancing from `seeded_at`
through each step to `clock`, sweeps, `until: now + ttl`). Every oracle runs the
prelude (`execute::world`) and compares its outcomes (`prelude-*` fields;
`store-postgres-prelude`); a device acquires at the seed clock and catches up by
one sync round after the server's prelude. The prelude is emitted first so no
rewrite moves its sites. `lean::generate` narrows half the cases outside the
model (projections, expiry) back into its fragment; the rest stay named
unsupported (`shape`, `loop`, `table-expiry`). The report's `coverage` counts
each new feature (`block/*`, `prelude/*`, `projection/*`, `expire/*`, `clock/*`).

Quarry device testing (`src/devices.rs`, `src/device_writes.rs`, LLP 3000.035
§5.1 oracle 4): each case runs on a server engine and on a device of each store
(native SQLite at a file path, and memory), both brought up through the client's
own path: the `/schema` backend as JSON text, then `local.ts::syncRound` (capture
`sync_state`, `/sync` snapshot pages built as `serve_sync.rs` builds them,
`observe_store`, `apply` through `call_text`, catch-up stream). Never seed a
device store directly. Reads the device publishes without the server (`complete`
with `unknown` false, or a known refusal) compare the whole outcome record
except `seq` (and server-only `delivery`); every other read counts under a named
reason (`online-only-*`). Low ceilings reach the device only through `call`'s
`spent` ledger (`default - n`), compared at the server's boundary positions.
Writes go through `admit`: a device refusal must equal the server's, a
predicted row must equal the committed one (less its `pending` marker), and
after `settle` plus a sync round the device must answer `observe` as the server
does. `run-devices` accepts `--seconds`. Known findings are retained under
`cases/found/device-*` with a `DIAGNOSIS.md`; `tests/devices.rs` replays them
and `tests/smoke.rs` pins the fixed-seed signature set.

The Lean oracle (`run-lean`, LLP 3000.035 §5.2): `snapback4_lang::emit::lean`
translates each generated program's surface tree (never the binder's IR) to
the model's case JSON; `quarry-oracle` (`lean/Oracle.lean`, one process per
worker) answers one tagged outcome per line; the engine runs on SQLite at
default ceilings. Compared: kind, refusal code, data (tagged: an id is not a
text), `complete`, `next` presence, each side's own continuation, and a
mutation's `observe` reread. Not compared: meter fields and sites. Programs
outside the model's fragment are named unsupported reasons, never passes.
`lean::generate` adds Lean-only variants (per-effect rules, a hidden probe
target, nullable/id orders, residual filters) aimed at `lean/OPEN.md`. A
disagreement is a Rust defect, a model defect (only when a document
contradicts the model: fix the model, rerun `lean/check.sh`), or an open
point (record the engine's behaviour in `OPEN.md`); never change the model to
match the engine without a document. Findings live in
`cases/found/lean--*` with `DIAGNOSIS.md`; `tests/lean.rs` replays them and
pins the open signature set. Lean-dependent tests skip loudly without the
built model; `SNAPBACK4_REQUIRE_LEAN=1` makes that a failure.

Quarry scheduled testing: prepare a separate clean clone whose current branch
can fast-forward to `origin/main`. The runner fetches/fast-forwards it and starts
its own socket-only evaluation cluster with `fsync=off`,
`synchronous_commit=off`, `full_page_writes=off`, `shared_buffers=1GB`, and
`max_connections=200`. It builds the Lean model's `quarry-oracle` first
(`lake build` in `lean/`; a host without `lake` fails the run), then runs the
SQLite, store, device and Lean campaigns on the selected
seed window, replays shrunk findings twice, and files/appends open `issues/*.md`
tickets. Only ticket changes are committed/pushed, with three fetch/rebase
retries. State and reports live outside Git under `--state-dir`; seeds advance
only after completed work and successful owned-cluster cleanup. Dirty/diverged
trees, overlap, setup failures, partial reports and failed publication refuse.
A crash can retain the lock and cluster directory; inspect `lock/owner.json`
and the run report. Never stop a cluster by process name.

`--dry-run --cases 32` writes previews and a separate `next-seed.dry-run.json`,
never commits or pushes. Dry runs may explicitly supply `--external-postgres
'host=... user=... dbname=...'`; that cluster is neither started nor stopped by
the runner. Ambient connections do not override normal private-cluster ownership.
The installer remains an operator action; do not invoke it during development.

The Lean oracle on a scheduled host (one-time, per user, no sudo): install
elan with `curl https://raw.githubusercontent.com/leanprover/elan/master/elan-init.sh -sSf | sh -s -- -y --default-toolchain none`.
The runner finds `lake` on `PATH` or in `~/.elan/bin`; the first `lake build`
downloads the toolchain pinned in `lean/lean-toolchain` (Lean 4.34.1, no
Mathlib), so the first scheduled run needs network. Check by hand with
`(cd lean && ./check.sh)` in the runner's clone. `run.json` records the pinned
toolchain and the oracle binary's digest.

# LLP 3000.013.001: Wave 12 semantic language gaps

**Type:** Spec
**Status:** Review
**Systems:** Snapback 4 Quarry parser, binder and type system; maintained views; core schema and interpreter; device stores; Lean model; differential generator; authoring guide
**Author:** GPT-5.6 Sol (for Charlie Cheever)
**Date:** 2026-10-14
**Revised:** 2026-10-15 (capture-time provenance and explicit scaled-division contract)
**Related:** [LLP 3000](./3000-snapback4.explainer.md), [LLP 3000.007](./3000.007-relaxed-quarry-and-explicit-residency.rfc.md) §§5.1–5.3, [LLP 3000.013](./3000.013-quarry-states-intent.rfc.md) §§3.2, 5.1, 14.7, [LLP 3000.019](./3000.019-what-the-builder-still-wrote.rfc.md) §3.2

## 1. Decision

Wave 12 adds five small language forms whose shared rule is that convenience
must not invent information. They use the existing interpreter, read-rule,
maintenance and transaction-fact machinery rather than parallel execution
paths.

1. `view total: count t` is a global maintained aggregate. Its group key is
   the empty tuple, so its target contains at most one physical row. Quarry
   reads it as the scalar name `total`. A readable missing row is the count
   identity, zero. A hidden row and a hidden miss are both null. Other
   aggregate kinds may use the same empty key, retaining their existing empty
   result semantics.
2. An exact successful positive-count guard proves that the same domain is
   non-empty until a
   write, a dependent-local rebind, an authority change or a control-flow
   join invalidates the fact. `min` and `max` become present only when their
   projected column is itself present; a non-empty population does not prove
   that an optional column has a non-null value. `sum` keeps its existing zero
   identity. A matching maintained-role guard may make the keyed result
   present through LLP 3000.013 §3.2's existing authority proof, but a write
   invalidates that proof. No guard turns hidden data into zero. Accepted
   comparisons are `count(domain) > k` for `k >= 0`, `>= k` or `= k` for `k
   >= 1`, and `!= 0`, plus their reversed forms.
3. `text ... format email` adds deterministic validation, not normalization.
   It accepts ASCII addresses of at most 254 bytes with exactly one `@`; a
   1–64 byte local part made from ASCII alphanumerics and
   ``.!#$%&'*+/=?^_`{|}~-`` (with neither edge nor two adjacent characters
   equal to `.`); and a 1–253 byte dot-separated domain whose 1–63 byte labels
   contain ASCII alphanumerics or interior `-`. A single domain label is
   allowed. Case and bytes are preserved. A malformed formatted argument
   refuses `E_INPUT`; inserting or updating a stored image that violates the
   declared format fails the ordinary column constraint with `E_CONSTRAINT`.
4. `search` and `matching` accept enum columns as well as text columns. Enum
   values use their declared string spelling and the existing word
   tokenizer/index. No enum coercion, hidden synonym or alternate ranking is
   added.
5. Rounded division has two explicit forms. `divide(dividend, divisor,
   rounding)` accepts a present `int`, `decimal S` or `money CUR S` dividend
   and a present `int` divisor, and keeps the dividend's type and scale.
   `divide(numerator, denominator, S, rounding)` accepts two present ints, a
   literal result scale `S` from 0 through 12, and returns `decimal S`; this is
   the direct fractional-average form. `rounding` in either form is the
   compiler-checked enum literal `toward-zero`, `away-from-zero`, `floor`,
   `ceiling`, `half-away-from-zero` or `half-even`. Division by zero refuses
   `E_DIV_ZERO`; an unrepresentable final i53 result or checked wide
   intermediate refuses `E_OVERFLOW`. Optional inputs must first be narrowed
   or coalesced; null is never treated as zero. Runtime evaluation uses signed
   integer quotient and remainder only—never floating point.

## 2. Rounded-division table

For the three-argument form let `x` be the dividend's stored integer. For the
four-argument form let `x = numerator * 10^S`, computed in a checked signed
wide integer without first imposing the i53 value bound. Let `q` be `x / d`
truncated toward zero, `r` its remainder, and `d` the divisor. When `r != 0`,
the direction away from zero is the sign of the exact quotient
(`sign(x) * sign(d)`).

| Mode | Adjustment from `q` |
| --- | --- |
| `toward-zero` | none |
| `away-from-zero` | one unit away from zero |
| `floor` | one unit toward negative infinity only for a negative exact quotient |
| `ceiling` | one unit toward positive infinity only for a positive exact quotient |
| `half-away-from-zero` | away only when `2 * abs(r) >= abs(d)` |
| `half-even` | away when greater than half; at an exact half only when `q` is odd |

The comparison is overflow-free in the implementation (it does not compute a
potentially overflowing doubled machine integer). Examples: `divide(5, 2,
'half-even') = 2`, `divide(7, 2, 'half-even') = 4`, `divide(-5, 2,
'half-away-from-zero') = -3`, `divide(5, -2, 'floor') = -3`, and
`divide(5, -2, 'ceiling') = -2`. Decimal and money values apply the same rule
to their exact stored minor-unit integer and retain their scale/currency.
The scaled form gives `divide(101, 2, 2, 'half-even') = 5050` (the decimal-2
value 50.50), `divide(1, 8, 2, 'half-even') = 12`, and
`divide(1, 8, 2, 'half-away-from-zero') = 13`; negative operands round with
the same signed rules. Scale zero is valid. Scale 12 is the maximum. Only the
rounded stored result must fit i53, so a wider intermediate such as
`divide(I53_MAX, I53_MAX, 12, 'half-even')` succeeds with
`1000000000000`.

## 3. Global maintained-view representation

The empty group is a real logical key, not a dummy author-visible column.
Physical stores still need an index component, so the generated target carries
one compiler-owned required boolean discriminator `$global = true`; its unique
`byGroup` index contains only that field. Quarry never exposes the field or
accepts it as a group key. Schema validation permits this exact target shape
only for an ungrouped maintain; user-declared empty indexes remain invalid.
Every aggregate writer uses the existing canonical maintained-row id function
over the logical empty tuple, so rebuild, activation and incremental updates
address the same row.

The scalar name lowers to a point read of that unique discriminator. It is not a
whole-table page and it consumes no arbitrary first row. Device completeness
and absence use that same unique key. Consequently public synced views can
prove readable absence and return zero, while private views retain null unless
the same authority proof that authorizes a keyed target is live.

## 4. Non-empty-domain proof

The binder records a count's canonical read domain at the instant the local
receives the count. That capture marker names the result's reaching definition
and is owned by both the result local and every stable value root used by the
read, including the transaction-state anchor. A successful positive-count
guard may publish a fact only while that exact definition marker remains live
on every owner. A later capture of the same textual domain has a different
definition and cannot revive the earlier result. The fact is keyed by the canonical
domain and matches only an identical table, selected index, keys, seeks and
filter expression after stable-value substitution.

Assignments clear the local's facts. Writes clear every count-capture marker,
the transaction anchor and all aggregate non-empty and maintained-authorization
facts. Authority changes clear the same capture markers before a later guard
can publish anything. Branch joins keep only facts present on every completing
path; loops reach the existing binding fixed point. Entering or leaving an
`as` viewer scope does not export the proof. Retained assignment origins remain
diagnostic history and are not provenance by themselves. This deliberately
misses some equivalent predicates; it must never accept a merely similar or
stale population.

The proof affects only static optionality. Runtime aggregates remain subject
to the existing meter/cut rule: no partial scalar escapes a cut. A later
write followed by an empty population therefore cannot reuse the earlier
proof, and an unauthorized maintained miss never becomes an authorized zero.

## 5. Compatibility and fences

`email` is a new closed schema enum tag and rounded division is a new closed IR
builtin tag. Older runtimes fail closed when decoding either. Existing schema
and program bytes are unchanged. Enum search and global views reuse existing
wire forms except for the deliberate one-component, compiler-owned `$global`
discriminator index; schema validation rejects that shape outside its exact
maintained target.

No feature adds JavaScript evaluation, a second interpreter, regular
expressions, floating point, unbounded scans or implicit disclosure.

## 6. Verification contract

Affected tests must cover:

- parsing, binding, schema validation and incremental maintenance of a global
  count, including zero, insert, delete and readable-versus-hidden absence;
- global-view replication and updates in both SQLite and memory device stores;
- matching count guards, mismatched domains, optional projected columns,
  branch joins, result and dependent-root rebindings, stale counts captured
  before writes, impure helper calls, authority edges, and fresh counts after
  writes;
- immediate keyed-role authorization, hidden hit/miss equivalence, readable
  zero, and invalidation by a following write;
- accepted and rejected email edge cases through both server and device
  validation;
- enum search planning, matching and replication on both stores;
- every rounding mode across positive and negative operands, exact halves,
  non-halves, result scales 0 and 12, the direct `101 / 2` decimal-2 average,
  a wide intermediate with a representable result, zero divisors and final
  i53 overflow, with no floating-point oracle;
- Lean evaluation and differential-case generation for rounded division;
  independent Lean witnesses for global-total presence/disclosure,
  count/role narrowing, email validation and enum word search; plus simulator
  and both device-store execution. Model boundaries remain explicit rather
  than reporting unsupported maintained/search execution as oracle coverage.

The guide's types, search, language and derived/maintained-view cards carry
the exact supported spellings and the presence/disclosure boundaries.

## Summary

Eighteen Clique calibrations sit on a plateau: holistic 88–92, with
`data_modeling`, `queries_and_live` and `scale_and_limits` at the bottom in
every window (LLP 3000.012 §2.1). Every `data_modeling` note charges the cost
of learning Quarry's execution model, and most charge a read model the
application maintains or a capacity number the author chose. 0.3.0 moved
three derived forms into the engine and the calibration did not move
(`data_modeling` 87, `queries_and_live` 90).

The remaining cost is the surface itself. A query names the index it scans
(`by byAuthorTime`), hand-merges lanes (`[h] for h in range(hour(now) - 24,
hour(now) + 1)`) and states bounds the engine could choose (`first 10001`,
`size authors 2000, edges 20000`, `cap 60000`). Each derived form has its own
grammar and its own limits. A typed reference can silently select a parent
scan instead of the row it names. The builder has to learn the engine's cost
model to state what the product means.

Charlie authorized significant rework (2026-09-23: "if you need to try making
*significant* architectural reworks in order to make the data modeling,
queries, and scalability be excellent and elegant, you can experiment with
that. I'm not attached to things being the way they are now."). This RFC
decides that rework:

1. **Reads state intent; a planner chooses how.** `posts where .authorId =
   owner last 20 by .at after c`. The compiler chooses or synthesizes every
   index. Queries, rules, sync lines, caps and expiry never name one.
   Time-window rankings become bucketed lane merges without authored lanes.
2. **One derived-data declaration, `view`.** The engine picks the strategy:
   filters, projections and unions are planned at read time; aggregates are
   maintained in the writing transaction; Following is materialized per
   reader.
3. **Following without caps.** Delivery to followers becomes engine-owned
   background work, so a post acknowledges in constant time. Reads hide
   unfollowed authors immediately. Promotion, pull routes, broadcast lanes and
   every author-visible cap leave the design.
4. **Work without bounds.** Aggregates over reads stream instead of
   materializing pages. Job loops chunk themselves. `emit … once` replaces
   marker tables.
5. **A paved client.** One app object owns sign-in, restore and the durable
   outbox. One command gives a web export an offline shell.

The engine, rules, partitions, prediction, metering and IR stay. The rework
is a planner and desugarer in front of the binder, three engine additions
(merge-lane projection, background delivery, streaming aggregates), and the
client.

## 1. Evidence

**Observed** (calibration #18, `benchmarks/runs/2026-09-23-snapback4-clique-astra-0.3.0/`):

| Category | Score | The scorer's charge |
|---|---:|---|
| data_modeling | 87 | "restrictive program shapes and unfamiliar compiler vocabulary"; "subtle reference-driven index selection" |
| queries_and_live | 90 | "Global needed a separate event table, and queries required explicit bounds and carefully shaped merges" |
| background_work | 89 | "atomic per-recipient digest computation potentially parking at job bounds" |
| client_integration | 92 | "Cold web launch required an authored app-shell service worker; native lifecycle evidence stops at builds" |
| scale_and_limits | 90 | "builder diagnostics, not the full independent probe matrix; finite work ceilings remain relevant" |

The builder's 542-line backend carries 25 `by` lines, 12 `sync` lines, eight
`cap` lines and a timeline `size` clause, none of them product rules except
`cap 50 by conversationId`. It also carries three application tables that
hold derived or bookkeeping state (`events`, `dmPairs`, `digestMarkers`) and
a hand-shaped 25-lane Trending merge. Its diary: "The difficult part was
understanding when a typed reference selects a parent index rather than an
id lookup." Its essay: the author must learn "a bounded prefix, a held query,
a maintained value, a source horizon".

An independent assessment (a separate Claude session, relayed by the author
on 2026-09-23) reached the same place from the design: the language shows
the engine's cost model instead of hiding it; the derived forms are separate
features that did not compose by default; the timeline carries sizing numbers
in application code; the next gains come from simplifying the core language.
What it said would change its answer: one general derived view that the
engine maintains; a planner, with bounds inferred and defaulted; data
modeling at parity with SQL on this brief; evidence beyond one app and one
builder.

**Interpretation.** The strongest categories (media 98, authorization 97)
are the ones where a declaration on a table does the whole job. The weakest
are the ones where the author must also say *how*. The fix is to let the
author say only *what*, everywhere, and to move the *how* into a planner and
the engine.

## 2. Reads state intent

### 2.1 Predicate reads

```quarry
query userPosts(owner: principal, c: cursor ?):
  return posts where .authorId = owner last 20 by .at after c postCard
query thread(postId: posts, c: cursor ?):
  return replies where .postId = postId first 20 by .at after c
query trending():
  return posts where .at > now - 1d and .at <= now last 10 by .likeCount, .at postCard
```

A read is `T where P`, optionally followed by `matching q`, a page clause
(`first N` ascending or `last N` descending), `by K1, K2, …` and `after c`,
then an optional shape. Order keys are columns (`.at`), including
engine-maintained columns. `id` is always the final tiebreak in the same
direction. Without `by`, the order is `id`. Ids are time-ordered, so
`last N` is newest first. Without a page clause the read is a domain: the
whole matching set, bounded as today by a schema cap or the meter, and
chunked in a job (§5.2).

Supervisor ruling (2026-09-24): in a table order, every key after `id` is
redundant because `id` is unique within that table. The planner truncates the
order at `id`: `by .id, .at` plans exactly as `by .id`, using the existing id
index without a duplicate component or new index. View orders are not
truncated: ids may coincide across branches, and branch identity breaks any
remaining tie after the projected order keys.

The planner splits `P` into top-level conjuncts:

| Conjunct | Plan |
|---|---|
| `.c = e`, with `e` independent of the row | an equality pin on `c` |
| `.c < e`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` on the first order key | a seek |
| a range on a `time` column other than the first order key, with finite lower and upper bounds (`now - D` and `now`, `D` constant) | bucketed lanes over every intersecting bucket: `hour` for a window ≤ 48h, `day` for ≤ 92d; the exact endpoints stay as filters, so the page is exact. With only one bound the window is not finite, and the read is an ordinary residual scan with a note that adds the missing bound |
| `.c in e`, with `e` a bounded list or one column of a read (`members where .principal = viewer`)`.conversationId` | one lane per value |
| anything else | a residual filter, evaluated after the read rule, under the meter |

The 0.4.1 Workroom ruling (2026-09-24) makes ordering comparisons on nullable
scanned-row columns inside `where` false on null. A seek on such a column
excludes nulls: an upper-only seek has an exclusive null lower bound.
Equality and inequality with null remain total. Nullable arguments/locals and
comparisons outside predicates keep their presence checks.
Seek extraction, including an explicitly ordered page, requires a present,
infallible endpoint before the predicate runs. Required bindings and literals
qualify; arithmetic qualifies only with a proof against overflow. Division and
optional bindings guarded within the predicate stay residual, preserving
short-circuit evaluation and narrowing.

Required enums of at most eight variants plan `!=` a literal or stable bound
value as membership in the remaining variants. Nullable enums and larger
enums remain residual; nullable inequality retains null rows. Fallible
exclusion expressions remain under their original predicate guards.
Value lanes require a proof that every lane prefix decides the source read
rule, including any nullable fallback lane. Otherwise membership and enum
inequality stay residual on an ordinary scan, preserving its continuation
through visible rows without claiming completeness for a non-uniform rule.
Certificates render residual membership as membership, not its lowered
boolean initializer; fully extracted predicates have no residual clause.

The optional-filter ruling (2026-09-24) recognizes `(a = null or C)` in
either disjunct order (also accepting `==` in this idiom). `a` must be an
optional argument or a local derived only from arguments. `C` must be a
pinnable equality, bounded membership, or range with a safe endpoint that
uses `a` and no other optional input. Up to three distinct inputs receive
presence alternatives; additional conjuncts remain residual and are named
by `N_OPTIONAL_FILTER_LIMIT`. Each alternative uses ordinary index planning
and admission. The runtime selects it before the scan, removing an absent
input's conjunct and narrowing a present input. Streaming aggregate
consumers remain streaming on each alternative. Certificates describe each
presence combination; any growing alternative makes the operation grow.

Presence alternatives share a logical page site and carry a fixed-size
128-bit identity in their opaque cursor scope. Changing presence refuses
with `E_CURSOR_INDEX`, including when alternatives share an index. A search
needle folding to no terms is another absence alternative: browse using the
ordinary pins and order. Evaluate the needle once and meter its fold before
choosing. This is Quarry lowering; serialized raw words-index IR keeps its
existing behavior when no word lanes exist. Server and device interpret
the same conditional reads. Generated browse normalization touches only its
outer leaf; nested point reads and needle expressions retain their own keys.
For an explicitly selected words index, the browse leaf reuses the
lexicographically first plain index with the identical effective ordering and
computed-key definition, or synthesizes its ordinary index. This generated
choice does not relax ambiguity checks on authored predicate reads. A unique
key with any nullable component is not a total cursor order: null ties are
legal. Browse alternatives and ordinary reads with cursors reuse an index
without a declared id only when every unique component is required (including
validated calendar keys). Otherwise they synthesize or choose a separate id
ordering, preserving the unique constraint. Explicit unsafe cursors refuse
with `E_CURSOR_INDEX` and a column-ordered read rewrite. Reads without cursors
may keep their existing physical-prefix indexes; merge cursors and internal
sweep/aggregate positions already carry the physical id tiebreak. The generated
Following inbox keeps its existing unique constraints and reads through a
separate `byReaderPage` index ending in id; pending-work completeness and
live-query dependencies apply to both old and new reader indexes.

Presence-selected reads cannot supply mutation population loops or top-level
job sweeps in this implementation. Bind those as an ordinary capped loop or
stable sweep and put the optional condition in its body. Mutation admission
retains conditional scan provenance even for emit-only loops. The runtime
validates every top-level loop before running any chunk and parks stored
non-native jobs with no recorded sweep or any unsupported work loop as
`E_JOB_SWEEP`. Mixed valid/invalid sweeps cannot skip work or commit a valid
chunk first. Bounded setup loops before a recorded sweep are supported when
both their bodies and domain expressions are write-free and emit-free;
compiler-generated prefix setup, such as a list `sum`, replays under each
chunk's meter. Inner loops keep their execution. A trailing setup loop with
no following sweep is unsupported because no chunk would execute it.

A keyed `exists` in a predicate is always an ordinary authorized point
probe when it covers a total unique key. Driving from that table is only
an optimization: if its discovery prefix cannot decide its read rule,
retain the point probe per candidate and explain the skipped-row growth.
The source rule, disclosure policy, scan admission and meter are unchanged.

The index is the pins in canonical order, then any bucket key, then the order
keys, then `id`. A declared index with exactly those leading components is
used. Otherwise the compiler synthesizes one and adds it to the schema. Its
identity derives from its complete canonical descriptor: components,
computed-key parameters, words fields and uniqueness. It is independent of
declaration and program order. `check --cost` prints
every chosen and synthesized index with the read that needs it. Index
synthesis changes nothing at run time. The engine builds indexes on adoption
exactly as it does for a declared `by` line.

A predicate read that the planner can only serve as a sparse residual scan
keeps today's note (`N_SPARSE_FILTER`), with a rewrite to a pin, a view
(§3), or an order key.

### 2.2 Point reads have one meaning

`T[e]` selects identity when `e` is typed `id` or a reference to `T`, even
when other one-column unique keys exist. It means `T[id = e]` and retains
the named form's table-identity check. Otherwise the argument types must
select exactly one declared unique key of the same arity, in declared column
order. A foreign-table reference may select a unique column of that reference
type; it cannot stand in for `T`'s identity. Principals and text select compatible
unique columns. Text literals retain contextual identity conversion, so a literal
may be ambiguous between identity and text keys. Exact type equality does not
break a tie between otherwise compatible declared keys. The same selection
applies to program reads, keyed writes and rule `exists`/`created` probes.
Explicit index names retain their existing semantics. Synthesized indexes never take part in resolving a
positional key, so adding a read can never change another read's meaning. `T[col = e, …]` reads by named
columns; named equalities that cover a total (non-nullable) unique key check
any extra columns on that one row. Equalities exactly covering a declared
unique key select a point even when columns are optional, in any order.
With the same selected unique index and no residual equalities, both lower
to the same `Get`/`Exists` key in declared column order; expression setup
retains authored evaluation order. A named read prefers
the shortest covered total unique key; with `unique single: low` and
`unique pair: low, high`, it may use `single` and check `high` afterwards,
while the positional pair uses `pair`. For admitted non-null arguments these
return the same row through different plans. A competing nonunique index
does not displace an exact unique key, including in rule probes.

**Calibration #31 (0.4.13), PK ruling 2026-10-06.** The first M3 check
reported four positional-read arity refusals, two positional-rule arity refusals
and one `conversations.slug is text <=80; got id` type error. The builder
removed conversation uniqueness; the resulting slug population carried
`N_NEVER_COMPLETE`. `data_modeling` scored 87 (calibration #30: 90). The lost
first draft is not claimed as preserved: the [PK report](../snapback4/reports/20261006-pk-typed-positional-keys/REPORT.md)
distinguishes reconstructed cases from the retained log. The old arity gate
counted implicit `byId`, so `unique slug` alone produced two candidates before
argument types were considered. Type-directed point selection removes that
pressure to weaken the schema while retaining NL's named and nullable rules.

**PK round 1 (2026-10-07).** Audience index planning consumes the ordinary
rule binder's admitted key and column order before synthesizing access indexes.
It must not repeat an arity-only choice: `exists members[.conversation, viewer]`
with `unique pair: conversation, principal` and
`unique reverse: principal, conversation` binds `pair` for both the rule and
sync planning. The content prefix, inverse discovery index and any horizon
order use that choice. Explicit and inferred sync audiences share it; nullable
proofs, declared provenance and genuine ambiguity remain unchanged. A reversed
probe binding viewer first retains the existing non-invertible sync refusal.

Program key selection retains the expressions and types already bound, then
uses them for final lowering; it must not recursively bind the whole key again
to discover its type. Setup and allocation stay once, in authored order,
including a positional prefix followed by named tests. Astra's round-0 review
found missing sync indexes and an eight-level typed identity query taking
9,030 ms versus 57 ms with explicit `byId`. Regressions compare inferred sync
schemas with explicit-index controls, require the nested query to compile in
under one second and check one runtime read per level and key evaluation order.
The [PK round-1 report](../snapback4/reports/20261006-pk-typed-positional-keys/REPORT.md#round-1--review-fixes-2026-10-07)
records the reproductions and compatibility differential.

**Nullable point admission (NL round 1, 2026-10-03).** Each argument for a
nullable column of the selected unique key must be provably non-null: a
non-optional static type or control-flow guard. This applies to positional
and named points, `exists` in programs and rules, and keyed write targets.
Otherwise `E_QUARRY_NULL_KEY` refuses compilation: null-bearing unique keys
permit several rows, and different replicas may hold different tied rows,
so choosing a first candidate cannot define a shared point contract. Guard
the arguments (`if x != null`, or `x != null and exists ...` in a rule),
read the population (`T where .low = x and .high = y by .id` with a page
bound or cap), or address a row by id. `created` probes follow the same
admission. Required-key null arguments still address nothing. Maintained
aggregate null groups are exempt and retain their existing group meaning.
Extra value predicates and secondary access indexes preserve that exemption
when every grouping column is pinned. An index that omits a grouping column
cannot claim it.

**Point probes (NL round 2, 2026-10-03).** The same replica split predates
NL for non-null ties on nonunique indexes. Compilation now refuses a point
probe whose selected key can match several rows (`E_QUARRY_POINT_KEY`),
including explicit `by`, rule `exists`/`created`, and final-insert probes.
A fully pinned superset of a required unique key is itself unique and remains
legal, including role-bearing access indexes used by existing postconditions.
A nullable unique constraint does not establish that unconditional proof;
select its unique index and prove its nullable arguments present instead.
This chooses compile-time admission rather than adding a bounded search to
point IR: population `exists` already supplies that search in code, including
unavailable scalar answers when a scan is cut. Rule probes require uniqueness.
This admission change leaves storage and population authorization unchanged;
Round 9 below also defends runtime point evaluation.

Planning must retain the original membership predicate as an admission
obligation before dropping its runtime probe. Binding checks it in the original
lexical and focal-row context before accepting the proposed lane, including
lanes nested in planned views. Scan predicates have a scoped focal binding:
short-circuit guards narrow its fields, and facts cannot escape to another row.
Point-key diagnostics explain the recovery choices but offer no executable
source edit without a context proof; the guide carries the general forms.
Index-mismatch and program/rule ambiguity diagnostics build candidates from
the caller's actual read and operands, never from index column names as
expressions. The shared repair verifier reparses the edited declaration and
binds it with the original project, including shape instantiations, helper
callers and job chunk contracts, without recursively verifying candidate
diagnostics. These index diagnostics arise in actual caller expansions; their
retained callers supply focal types, execution mode and placement. No extra
query is added to test a mutation helper. The declaration-local parser-repair
path, which retains no callers, still checks helpers through a typed synthetic
query with an unspellable compiler-only name; standalone shapes there have no
focal proof and offer no repair. Only a clean compilation permits a source
rewrite. This includes point and range alternatives and a fully pinned range's
possible point replacement. A positional key matching several type-compatible
declared unique indexes (`E_QUARRY_POSITIONAL_SCAN`) names each candidate as a
copy-pasteable named form using the caller's operands. When indexes share the
same columns in different orders, the form also names the index. `check --fix`
may apply the first context-verified candidate; this is an explicit opt-in to
that choice, not a claim that the compiler knows the author's intended key.
The ordinary check still refuses ambiguity. Unknown explicit index names keep
NL's verified alternative-index suggestions. Types, bounds, nullable admission
and the original callers must pass before a rewrite is offered. Keyed writes
verify the edited target inside their original mutation and retain its payload.
Unspellable planner tokens, unproved nullable points, invalid chunk sketches and mismatches without
a verified alternative get no source template, only prose guidance. Independent
errors in that context can also withhold a candidate. The point-admission
diagnostics themselves keep empty rewrites.

Storage uniqueness and total equality are unchanged: null equals null,
and bounded `where` reads can return every visible null match. A verified
repair of a `where` population over an exact nullable unique key must retain
a population: keep an existing valid page repair; for an otherwise bare key,
try `by .id` and verify its existing bound, or offer no rewrite. Never offer a
bare point or truncate ties with `first 1`. A fully pinned nonunique index is
not reused for a page: the planner supplies the unpinned `id` component needed
by the range binder. This does not make a nullable unique key a total cursor
order (§2.1).

A positional read that would select a non-unique prefix without an explicit
`by <index>` is refused, with the `where` rewrite. This removes type-directed
selection between a row and a parent scan. Explicit `by <index>` ranges remain
accepted; point probes must satisfy the uniqueness admission above.

**2026-10-03 (QE2):** an identical unique-key lookup is non-null after
`require exists T[k]` or `require T[k] != null`, and inside the present
`if T[k] != null` branch. Stable keys, lexical joins and write invalidation
bound this fact to unchanged transaction state (LLP 3000.007 §5.2). Required
references do not establish existence; membership guards need an explicit
parent guard even when they match the parent's read rule.

**2026-10-14 (wave 11, client result inference):** postfix `!` on a
unique point establishes the same presence witness as an existence guard.
A same-table update preserves that witness only for ordinary tables without
expiry, opening bounds, through authority or ephemeral lifetime, when neither
the selected unique key nor any additional named equality changes, and the
read rule's deciding fields remain unchanged. A previously proved,
row-independent read disjunct, such as an explicit moderator-roster guard,
also preserves readability when another disjunct's fields change. Self-table
probes, maintained columns and maintained probe dependencies remain conservative. Deletes, inserts,
upserts, writes to other tables, helper writes and compound effect barriers
still clear these witnesses. Branch joins and lexical rebindings retain the
existing fact intersection and root-revision rules.

A direct update/upsert result is required only when the same ordinary lifetime
boundary holds and its final read grant is unconditional or proved by an
unchanged row-independent disjunct. An absent update target and a false update
condition refuse; neither is a successful null result. Private blind writes,
expiry, opening bounds and through authority retain nullable final-read
results. This changes inferred types, never authorization, write execution or
wire outcomes. The compiler suite compares emitted TypeScript and engine
results, including authority loss, unique-key/equality changes, branch joins,
deletes, other-table writes, expiry and unopened upserts.

**2026-10-04 (NL round 8 / QE2 integration):** bind and admit the guard's
point before recording its presence fact. An unproved nullable unique key in
`require exists T[k]` still refuses `E_QUARRY_NULL_KEY`; guard `k != null`
first. Successful existence narrows the row, not its optional fields. A
required field of that proved row can supply a non-null argument to another
nullable unique point. Rule guards also track one-hop reference terms in
write rules (LLP 3000.007 §5.4), including their old/next image selector.
A guard on `old.parent.low` cannot prove `next.parent.low` present. These
facts grant neither read-rule hops nor final-insert hops; their existing
`E_QUARRY_RULE_HOP` boundaries remain intact.

**2026-10-04 (NL round 9 / QE2 rule lifetimes):** ordinary unique-key points
with any null argument return no row (`exists`/`created`: false) on server and
device before storage access, independently of null-tie count or expiry.
Source admission still requires proof for nullable columns; maintained null
groups and population equality retain their separate semantics. Rule guard
facts describe the logical edge where an operand can affect truth, not a
promise of physical short-circuiting. Whole-rule expiry accounting may evaluate
the other edge too (LLP 3000.015 §2): the runtime null guard makes that extra
probe a known false result without a scan, meter cut or tie-derived lifetime.
Reference-term lifetimes are still evaluated, and non-null probes retain their
existing authorization, meter and expiry paths. Old/next selector identity and
the scope of presence facts are unchanged.

### 2.3 No index names anywhere

`by` lines on tables become optional tuning. The compiler synthesizes what
each of these needs:

- rule probes (`exists members[.conversationId, viewer]`, named probes);
- sync audiences and horizons: `sync to members[.conversationId] last 500 by .at`;
- `cap N by col`;
- `expire at .expiresAt`, whose sweep index is synthesized;
- word search. A table line `search displayName, handle` declares the words,
  and `matching q` reads synthesize the words index for their pins and order.
  A matching page may also derive that order from a declared plain unique
  index, with bracket keys restricted to its leading prefix (LLP 3000.007 §18.1).

`unique` takes an optional name: `unique handle else HANDLE_TAKEN 'That
handle is taken.'`, `unique postId, principal`.

### 2.4 Durations

`500ms`, `30s`, `15m`, `24h` and `7d` are integer milliseconds in any
expression, not only in `bucket` and `schedule`.

## 3. One derived-data form: `view`

A view is a named query. The engine decides whether to plan it at read time,
maintain it, or materialize it. `maintain … : timeline` and `maintain
name: count …` remain accepted as older spellings, and `check --fix` rewrites
them.

### 3.1 Planned views: filter, projection, union

```quarry
view activity:
  posts where not .removed { post: .id, actor: .authorId, at, repost: false }
  reposts { post: .postId, actor: .actorId, at, repost: true }

query global(c: cursor ?):
  return activity last 20 by .at after c { *, post: posts[.post] postCard, actor: profiles[principal = .actor] }
```

Each branch is `T [where P] { fields }`. Every branch yields the same field
names with compatible types. A view row's identity is its branch and its
source row's `id`: ids are unique within a table, not across tables. So two
branches never collapse into one row, and cursors carry the branch.
A view is read like a table. A pin or range on a view field becomes a pin or
range on each branch's source column. A pin on a constant field selects the
matching branches. Order keys must be source columns in every branch.

The plan is one merge lane per branch, and per `in` value or bucket. Each lane
scans its own table under that table's read rule, applies the branch filter,
then projects. The merge orders by the projected order keys, then source id
if absent from those keys, then branch identity. The cursor carries those
values. Source ids may coincide across branches; branch identity keeps those
rows distinct, with no duplicates or gaps across tables. Nothing is stored.
Live queries, devices and prediction behave exactly as for the source tables.

**Engine addition:** `MergeLane` gains an optional projection, evaluated per
row after the read rule and filter, before merging. Lanes may name different
tables. The merge key is read from the projected row. The existing
cross-table cursor translation (LLP 3000.007 §20.3) generalizes to
projected lanes.

### 3.2 Maintained views: aggregates

```quarry
view followerCount: count follows by .followedId
view receivedLikes: count likes by .postId.authorId
view dailyPosts: count posts where not .removed by .authorId, day(.at)
view revenue: sum orders of .amount by .shopId

table posts:
  likeCount: count likes
```

These have exactly the semantics of today's maintains: the same engine, the
same recorded attribution, and maintained columns for the in-table form.
`followerCount[p]` reads the number, 0 when absent. Two defaults remove the
boilerplate lines:

- **Readability is derived.** A uniformly readable source gives a readable
  aggregate. A source whose read rule uses only bare group keys gives the same
  rule over the aggregate's key. Anything else needs an explicit `read <-`.
- **In-table columns find their reference.** A column is counted by the one
  column of the source that references the table. If there are several, use
  `count likes by .postId`.

### 3.3 Materialized views: Following

```quarry
view following: activity where .actor = viewer or exists follows[viewer, .actor]

query home(c: cursor ?):
  return following last 20 by .at after c activityCard
```

The planner recognizes this shape and materializes one inbox per reader. It
does so only when materializing discloses nothing the sources do not already
disclose. The originals, reposts and edges must be explicitly public and
fully `sync public`, with owner rules and immutable mapped columns, as the
0.3 timeline requires. Structure alone is not permission; private feeds
would need their own per-recipient authorization design.

- a planned union with an originals branch (`post: .id`, a principal actor
  column, a time column, an optional one-way removal flag);
- a reposts branch (`post:` a reference to the originals table);
- filtered by the viewer plus an edge table whose unique key is `(follower,
  followed)` of principals.

The declaration contains no sizes, no author table and no caps. Any other view
that mentions `viewer` is planned at read time.

## 4. Following without caps

The 0.3 timeline copies events inside the writer's transaction. To keep that
work under the 1,024-write mutation ceiling, it promotes authors past 50
followers to a shared broadcast lane. It merges at most 32 such lanes on
read, and it caps follows, followers, authors and events. Each of those
numbers exists only because the fan-out runs synchronously.

This RFC makes delivery engine-owned background work:

| Transition | In the writing transaction | Afterward |
|---|---|---|
| Post or repost | the source row, the author's own inbox copy, one durable delivery record | copies to followers, 256 per chunk |
| Follow | the edge, plus copies of the author's newest 50 events | older events, chunked |
| Unfollow | the edge delete | deletion of that author's copies, chunked |
| Remove (one-way flag) | a public tombstone | purge of copies |

Reads filter the inbox by the view's own predicate: the actor is the viewer
or is still followed. That is one point probe per candidate row. Unfollow
therefore takes effect on the next read. It also deletes up to 256 stale copies
in its own transaction, so an ordinary unfollow leaves nothing to skip.
Removal hides through the tombstone, as today.

Every task is durable and idempotent:

- Delivery, backfill, cleanup and purge are enqueued in the transaction that
  causes them.
- A task's progress commits with the rows it writes.
- SQLite disk transactions use WAL `synchronous=FULL`, including background
  work. A chunk also publishes partition-log watermarks: replaying lost copies
  would not repair a watermark already observed by a device. `NORMAL` is
  therefore insufficient even for idempotent delivery.
- Copies are admitted by their (reader, event) identity.
- Tasks are bound to the incarnation of their edge and event. An old cleanup
  never deletes copies made by a refollow. Delivery revalidates the event and
  each edge in every chunk. A tombstone outlives any task that could still
  publish its event.

Background delivery runs on the server promptly after the commit that
enqueued it, not on a minute schedule. Followers normally see a new post
within a second; the author sees it immediately. Following pages over
*delivered* inbox contents:

- A page read during an unfinished delivery may lack the newest foreign
  events.
- `complete` is false for a reader while a backfill or cleanup task for that
  reader is pending.
- Nothing the predicate excludes is ever shown.
- `doctor` lists pending tasks.

There are no author modes, pull routes, pull counts, broadcast lane or
author-visible caps. The per-chunk meters bound engine work. Devices hold the
reader's private inbox and the public edges, and apply the same read filter
locally.

The server admits requests and maintenance through a FIFO. Maintenance may
wait for 1 ms without request activity, but takes its ticket after at most
5 ms of deferral, so sustained traffic cannot starve it. If requests are already
queued behind the active request, it joins the queue immediately. It uses a 250 µs
cooperative work slice when contended and 2 ms otherwise, in addition to the
count and meter bounds. These slices end between atomic rows; commit I/O can
extend the lock hold. A request already queued precedes the next chunk.

**2026-10-02 host scheduling update (CT round 4).** The engine FIFO remains.
All engine/writer holders now keep ordinary priority, superseding round 3's
utility/nice-5 bulk thread after the shared-gate inversion review. Bulk pauses
between slices under request/host contention; recounts yield between rows and
native invocations retain an explicit atomic resource bound. No maintenance
gate spans engine admission. LLP 3000 §7 “Contended read serving” records the
ordering, clock-drain exclusion and aged minimum service. The single-thread
statements below describe that historical run, not the current host.

**2026-10-04 LU round 1 update.** Background turns append unfinished work
and new arrivals behind all pending items, using the existing durable work
queue position. An item among P pending items receives a slice within P visits
to its declaration (D×P successful delivery turns across D declarations), even
with continuing arrivals. LLP 3000 §7 states the proof, restart scope and
wall-clock limitations. This supersedes round 0's starvation-prone forward-key
rotation. Later events may arrive before earlier events; pages still sort the
delivered contents by declared event order and deduplicate by event identity.
Admission, epochs, read authority and completeness are unchanged.

**2026-10-04 LU round 2 update.** Following walks grow their scan page from
two candidates only while the slice can consume more, capped at 32. The
256-row chunk, cursor atomicity, P-visit share and cooperative deadlines are
unchanged. CT's empty-kind CPU is repaid with the next useful slice, when
accumulated debt reaches 100 ms, or before an empty cycle's idle wait. Each
kind's charge and each repayment keep the 100 ms cap; unpaid debt carries
forward. Cheap empty kinds avoid separate wakeups during fan-out.
LLP 3000 §7 and the LU report bound this policy and its measured completion
claims; finite fan-out still requires proportional work.

**2026-10-04 RP integration.** Enqueuing synchronous Following work reserves
one examined row, one index entry, eight steps and reusable scratch of eight
times the owned Work row's copy ceiling on both hosts. Only the server looks
up the durable queue tail; the device creates no Work row. The existing shared
hidden-write reservation uses the maximum-width queue position when pricing
output, so a private tail or a rewound clock cannot change prediction admission.
Background rotation still uses its ordinary metered lookup and commits its
new queue position with the cursor.

**Ten-CPU measurement, 2026-09-29 (lane BP).** Retain this policy. Delivery,
view recounts and jobs already share one maintenance thread; a pending task
is not a runnable worker. All 167,157 calibration actions replayed with server
and client confined to Linux CPUs 0–9. The several-fold Mac curve did not
reproduce: warmed full/small p95 ratios were 1.057 for history, 1.014 for
Following/500, 1.132 for search and 1.592 for Insights. Following still had
36,569 pending tasks after the full probes. The warmed search/trending midpoint
rules failed by 0.482/0.511 ms; no batch or ceiling was changed.

Requests retained sub-millisecond median admission and microsecond reader
checkout during those probes. The one maintenance thread consumed 282.38 CPU
seconds across replay and drain, almost all in Following; queued task count
did not turn into parallel background CPU consumption. Host CPU occupancy was
sampled, not assumed idle: warm probe windows observed roughly 29–34% of the
ten-CPU capacity, while other intervals reached 97%. The three-empty-sample
final drain took 168.27 seconds after replay/verification returned. The existing
5 ms admission deferral and cooperative chunk budgets do not bound an entire
backlog's delivery latency. No concurrency, OS priority/QoS, batching, meter,
durability or operator-setting change follows from this non-reproduction.
See [BP's report](../snapback4/reports/20260929-bp-foreground-first/REPORT.md)
for every batch, host-load and request/thread record, snapshot/version limits,
and the build-free Mac replay handoff. Ten homogeneous Linux cores do not
recreate Apple's heterogeneous cores or the calibration's concurrent browser.

Removing a materialized view retires its owned rows, indexes and delivery work
in the activation transaction. Dependent aggregates are reset or retired there
too, including when their table names survive as ordinary tables. Source rows
and unrelated views survive. Dev needs no flag; deploy requires
`--allow-destructive`, as for removing a maintained aggregate.

Redefinition remains refused with `E_TIMELINE_REDEFINE`. A first-use declaration
can now start over populated sources under [LLP 3000.026 §4](./3000.026-following-over-a-populated-store.rfc.md#4-atomic-launch-adoption):
one activation transaction copies all retained own events and newest 1,000 live
events per current follow, without refill after removal. Dev adopts automatically;
deploy requires `--allow-feed-adoption`, prints its count/lock estimate, and
refuses before starting above 5,000,000 copies. Original ids remain post ids;
repost ids use a fresh adoption incarnation. Historical edge epochs, delivery
and removed-event history cannot be reconstructed; launch may include older
events a historical inbox never received. Retire a changed view, then use a fresh
owned/slot namespace or the planned `home` query in `guide feeds`. An unfinished
withdrawn experimental reconstruction still refuses to open or resume; removal
can retire it. The future online publisher in LLP 3000.026 §8 remains unbuilt.

## 5. Work without bounds

### 5.1 Streaming aggregates

`count(R)`, `sum(R, .col)` and `exists R`, where `R` is a predicate read
without a page clause, examine rows under the examined and steps meters.
Each decoded row is charged transiently, and exactly that charge is released
when the row is dropped. Retained state stays charged.

A streaming consumer keeps the underlying scan's admission, authorization,
expiry and coverage checks. Calling a scan `count` does not make it a safe
probe; LLP 3000.007 §21.9's expiring-mutation counterexample stands.
Unpaged aggregate reads retain ordinary streaming scans: membership, enum
complements and window predicates do not become bounded merge pages. Their
residual filters fold the entire admitted domain, or return null on a cut.
Streaming aggregation across planned lanes is not implemented.

The busy-chat digest claim (LLP 3000.011.001.000's 16 MiB stop) holds only
if the retained recipient-heavy fixture passes.

An inferred aggregate seek must preserve predicate short-circuiting: its
endpoint must already be present and must not fail when evaluated before the
whole predicate. Otherwise the comparison stays a residual filter. Selecting
one safe endpoint must not extract an unsafe sibling bound on the same column.
A named prefix pinning intrinsic `id` keeps its single-row access path; remaining
comparisons filter that row rather than introducing an order after the id pin.

### 5.2 Self-chunking jobs

A top-level `for x in R:` in a job, over a stable domain, is a chunked sweep.
A stable domain orders by `id` or by immutable columns; a row could otherwise
move behind the cursor. The engine commits every K iterations, with the cursor
and the evaluated domain bounds, as `chunk` does today.

K adapts: it starts at 64, and a meter refusal or internal physical
authorization-budget exhaustion retries the same uncommitted work with K
halved. Ordinary rule denials, constraint and generation refusals park at once.
A budget refusal parks only when a single iteration alone cannot fit. Physical
authorization exhaustion preserves its public E_RULE diagnostic at that point
(LLP 3000.007 §21.12); public meter exhaustion remains E_BOUND.

Locals declared in the loop body are per-iteration; loop-carried state
across a commit is refused. `chunk … first N` remains the explicit spelling.

### 5.3 Effects keyed once

`emit notify { … } once [p.principal, periodEnd]` records at most one effect
per effect name and key, forever. A repeat is a no-op, not a refusal, and
survives restart and retry. Keys are stored apart from the outbox, so a
replay-suppressed emit still records its key. `once` deduplicates emission,
not completion: an iteration that emits nothing records no key.

## 6. A paved client

- **The app object.** `snapback4/app` exports `createApp({ url, device?,
  sessionStore? })`. It returns `{ client, auth }`, where `auth.state` is
  `restoring`, `signed-out` or `signed-in`, and `auth` has `signup`,
  `login`, `logout` and `guest`. It persists the session and reopens the
  local outbox. Pending writes keep their ids across restarts without
  authored intent storage. In React, `<AppProvider app>` and `useAuth()`
  compose with the existing hooks. Client opening is provisional; the prior
  owner remains live until success. Replacement journals retirement, then
  commits the bearer and epoch in one atomic store write under the session
  lock. Automatic rotation and outbox replay start after that commit.
  Restoration and rotation retain their epoch; replacement of a live bearer
  advances it. Logout atomically writes a noncredential tombstone carrying
  the epoch and retirement obligations. In the browser, IndexedDB is the
  authoritative session state (2026-09-25 ruling): every session replacement or
  logout awaits its strict transaction commit inside the session Web Lock.
  localStorage mirrors that value and synchronously captures mutation intent;
  it is not authority for a locked admission or recovery check. Chromium's
  renderer caches can remain stale across Web Lock holders. A stale mirror may
  capture a click, but admission checks IndexedDB under the lock and returns
  `E_AUTH` instead of admitting or sending it after logout. Legacy mirror-only
  sessions require sign-in, and unadmitted records without the new authority
  stamp cannot be promoted; already committed outbox custody remains intact.
  Before opening a scope, the session lock protects migration of the maximum
  legacy mirror and IndexedDB epoch into IndexedDB and the epoch mirror. This
  imports an epoch fence, never credentials. Authoritative reads repair the
  session mirror, including deleting it for absent authority. A locked admission
  refusal schedules the app's authorization check after releasing the lock, so
  a confirmed stale scope also loses its observations. Every browser journaled
  write retains its original store binding until it leaves the outbox, including
  fresh clicks captured while startup validation is in flight; adoption of a
  replacement backend retires them without dispatch.
  **Busy-group authority reads (BG, 2026-10-02).** Each ordinary app authority
  check reads the legacy epoch marker and the session record in one fresh
  IndexedDB read transaction under that same session lock. It awaits transaction
  completion, repairs both mirrors best-effort, observes the maximum epoch and
  checks the same principal/tombstone fences before releasing the lock. This
  replaces three database opens/transactions (including a duplicate session
  read), without sharing results between checks or trusting mirror credentials.
  Opening/migration, strict writes and journal admission retain their existing
  procedures. The public residency before/after checks require two locked read
  transactions rather than six; the peer-logout, stale-mirror and failed-commit
  browser tests still govern the fence. See the
  [BG qualification](../snapback4/reports/20261001-bg-busy-group-render/REPORT.md).
  **BG round 1:** on an open IndexedDB-authority scope, overlapping facade/transport
  calls queued before its read starts may share that check's linearization point. The pending batch is
  cleared before lock acquisition; any call arriving during or after the read
  queues a new fresh transaction. No completed verdict is reused. Transaction
  completion, mirror repair, immediate epoch fencing, strict session writes and
  journal admission keep their existing requirements. This removes duplicate
  concurrent reads without extending authority past a later logout. Memory/native
  stores and preparing scopes retain their original per-call awaited persistence
  scheduling: a later held journal admission cannot overtake the first request's
  authority check.
  All browser handoffs toward delivery share this binding check, including
  orphan-tab adoption. Unknown destination identity defers a bound orphan in
  its source store; mismatch retires it before enqueueing. Ordinary and
  keepalive requests carry the original `store_id`, so server validation before
  execution and deduplication also fences replacement after client validation.
  A server `E_STORE_REPLACED` retires the write with that named refusal.
  An overlapping ordinary request owns settlement for its id, so a keepalive
  refusal cannot override its committed success. A keepalive refusal without
  that owner rechecks terminal history and outbox custody in the serialized
  device transaction, then commits the receipt and retirement atomically.
  An aborted receipt transaction retains custody and publishes no refusal.
  A known local terminal outcome, sent or failed, is never replaced. If its
  receipt save aborts, persist it before sync, replay or replacement handling
  touches that id. A retry with a known receipt settles it locally with the
  original sequence/refusal instead of issuing another POST.
  The exception is an unknown-outcome `E_STORE_REPLACED`: a success-qualified
  `sent_seq` or `observed_seq` proves success. Discard its unpersisted refusal
  before saving, and overwrite an existing replacement-refusal receipt only
  when the device transaction verifies the matching qualified outbox sequence.
  Stream acknowledgement lookup includes only `_ops` rows whose stored outcome
  is `sent`; the additive `sent` map carries that qualification as id → sequence.
  The device retains the qualifier with the outbox binding and exposes it only
  when that sequence is published. Legacy sequence-only observations, including
  ones previously promoted to `sent_seq`, prove a decision without its outcome.
  With no known terminal receipt, they remain pending and retain custody until a
  same-id POST to the original store returns its recorded outcome. This replay
  may correct an unknown replacement refusal to sent or failed; the persistence
  transaction verifies the original binding before replacing stored history.
  On both web transports, the retained receipt binding takes precedence over
  the journal binding and the device's current identity. Adoption shares a
  durably verified correction over an existing `E_STORE_REPLACED` in place
  before deleting its source, preserving receipt retention order.
  A caller's lookup of an id this device holds no outbox entry for applies the
  same rule: shared history recovers an absent receipt or a verified outcome
  answers over the reader's own `E_STORE_REPLACED`; every other local outcome
  answers first. Lookup rechecks custody after the shared read and recomputes
  through local custody if adoption added an entry. Settlement reads strictly
  this device's own history, even when the id is absent. The opener reads shared
  ids only to remember used mutation ids and route retries through lookup;
  it never copies or settles the shared outcomes.
  Neither qualified evidence nor replay replaces authored refusals such as
  `NOT_ADMIN`, or refreshes receipt retention. Native devices advertise
  `receipt_outcomes`; a JavaScript upgrade refuses an older module until rebuilt.
  Delivery receipts and outcome-qualified outbox sequences establish terminal custody;
  a local admission-storage error with an unknown outcome does not, and must
  leave the captured intent recoverable.
  Epoch migration
  writes only when the legacy mirror advances authoritative state; ordinary
  restoration needs no separate epoch allocation, and repairs mirrors
  best-effort even when localStorage is full.
  Every revocation path compares the
  currently stored bearer; a failed operation cannot revoke it or advance its
  epoch. Observing a newer epoch fences every older scope, including rollback
  candidates, before publication. A known server refusal conditionally
  tombstones the still-stored bearer or its known consumed predecessor after a
  failed rotation save, so later offline opens cannot reopen its replica.
  Auth state, viewer and client agree at auth and client callbacks. Hiding an
  account permanently fences exposed facades and observations independently of
  private raw retry custody; rollback exposes a new facade rather than reviving
  a previously hidden handle. A facade fence refuses new dispatches without
  replacing the outcomes of already-dispatched mutations, actions, uploads or
  refreshes. Close completes after local cleanup without waiting for a held network
  response, including unread session rotations. Already-started session persistence
  finishes locally; a late unkept successor is retired. Each mutation/action
  invocation whose response is received before public app close completes retains
  its full known outcome, including during session cleanup; otherwise the caller receives pending with its id. Requests
  are never aborted; later bodies are consumed and discarded. Durable mutation
  intent settles on reopen through the server's idempotency record. Within a runtime, mutation results, receipt lookup and
  notifications agree on each known terminal outcome, even when receipt saves
  keep failing. Online custody retains an unpersisted receipt summary in memory
  and notifies once; lookup retries persistence without reporting pending. The
  original online durable intent records its dispatch store before dispatch.
  Fresh online admission first probes an unidentified runtime and saves the
  returned store identity with its intent; a journal left by a replaced store
  cannot classify newly submitted intent as recovered unbound work. Recovered
  intents retain their original binding and strict first-store guard.
  A failed receipt save permits same-id replay only to that store; a persisted
  terminal receipt is not reposted. The server checks the requested store before
  execution and idempotency lookup, closing the probe/dispatch replacement race.
  On reopen a mismatched intent is retired with an unknown-outcome refusal.
  Unbound intent, including admission not yet marked dispatched, may replay only
  to the first store the journal has seen.
  Failed identity persistence blocks dispatch. Summaries never recover historical
  result values. Query data and observation snapshots
  remain fenced at delivery.
  Closing releases queued auth network waits without aborting revocation or
  discarding its late acknowledgement custody.
  Global logout awaits its own in-flight rotation and selects the stored bearer
  for the intended principal and calling epoch under the lock, including a
  peer's rotated successor. A stale caller cannot select a later login's epoch,
  even when its principal matches. Selection reads both inline and journaled
  principal watermarks directly under the existing session lock, and compares
  the selected session's committed scope rather than the raw shared counter.
  Only a committed tombstone hides the account; an earlier persistence failure
  keeps the signed-in view and reports why. The tombstone binds global retirement
  to that principal and generation, so late rotation responses inherit it and
  ordinary retirement cannot consume them first. Completed generation watermarks
  prevent stale tabs from recreating an acknowledged obligation or revoking a
  later login. Backend-bound retirement survives restart. Ordinary retirement
  accepts a logout acknowledgement or HTTP 401 E_AUTH; global retirement
  requires a successful logout-all acknowledgement. Each attempt freezes its
  credential coverage at dispatch; acknowledgement cannot erase retirement for
  tokens attached later, which retain individual custody. I1–I13 and their fair-recovery
  assumptions are recorded in the client reference and checked by 5,000 seeded
  three-runtime sequences per tier (online and the actual Rust/Wasm local
  client), including terminal mutation refusals, held outcomes across close,
  persistent online receipt-save failures and receipt lookups/notifications,
  with held storage, offline reopen and external
  server revocation, captured client handles, retained observations and failed
  rotation saves as well as auth operations, external sibling sessions and
  cross-tab global logout before/during rotation, held requests before issuance,
  and independent retirement transport failures. I9 covers all sessions at the
  server's global-revocation point, not deliberate new sign-ins afterward.
  A forcibly lost process or response while
  no storage/revocation succeeds cannot recover an unknown minted successor;
  that stronger guarantee requires a server issuance-recovery protocol. If all
  refusal-fence writes fail before process loss, a later offline runtime cannot
  distinguish the remaining bytes from a valid session. Lost global revocation
  acknowledgements also require server-side receipts for durable result recovery;
  E_AUTH alone does not prove global success. These limits are explicit in the
  client reference; no authorization or disclosure guarantee is weakened to
  simulate durable evidence that the client cannot obtain.
- **The offline shell.** `npx snapback4 web-shell <dir>` writes a service
  worker that precaches an exported web app (`expo export -p web` or a Vite
  `dist/`) and serves its shell offline, and registers it in `index.html`. The
  starters call it from their web build scripts.

### 6.1 Personas behind the App shape (wave 1, 2026-10-11)

The 0.4.16 app farm (100 agents, one new app each) found no persona path for
a React or Expo UI in 14 lanes (103 minutes): `AppOptions` omitted `persona`
on purpose ("identity belongs to app.auth"), so a `?as=bob` dev picker had to
abandon `AppProvider`/`useAuth` for `createLocalClient`/`createClient` plus
`SnapbackProvider`, found by reading `.d.ts` files.

`createApp({ url, persona, device? })` now acts as `dev:<persona>`. A persona
has no session, so this opener (`app-persona.ts`) is separate from the
session machinery above: no restoration, epochs, rotation, revocation journal
or session store. `app.auth.state` goes `restoring` to `signed-in` (viewer
`dev:<persona>`) or `signed-out` with `why`. `signup`, `login`, `guest` and
`logoutEverywhere` refuse `E_AUTH`; `logout` stops the app, and the persona's
device store (named per viewer) keeps its queued writes for the next app that
opens it. `app.online` reads as the persona. `readOnly` with a persona is still
refused (`E_READ_ONLY_CREDENTIAL`).

The server remains the boundary: `snapback4 dev` admits the header only from a
loopback socket, `Host` and `Origin`, and `serve` refuses it. The client adds
two earlier refusals so the failure is legible: a url whose host is not a
literal loopback name (`localhost`, `127.x`, `::1`; never DNS) or a persona
that is not a name resolves `ready` to `{ ok: false }` with `E_AUTH` before any
request carries the header; and the online tier probes `/probe` before
announcing `signed-in`, so `serve`'s refusal becomes `signed-out` with its
message rather than a signed-in app whose every read is denied (the device tier
already refuses while loading the backend). Writes keep the tier's own custody:
the device outbox and, in a browser, the web journal. As of wave 8,
device-less persona apps use the principal journal of LLP 3000.013.000 §17
when nothing syncs or with writes: "online"; close/logout preserve pending
intent for the same persona. The facade's `close`/`signOut` are not patched (pending-intent
registrations key the raw client), so `app.close()` and `app.auth.logout()` own
the lifetime. The client-card type fixture now accepts `persona` and still
rejects `guest` and `session`. Recipe: "Personas in a React UI" in
CLIENT-AND-OPERATIONS.md; tests: `app-persona.test.mjs`.

### 6.2 The online browser tier keeps the device (wave 1 assessment, 2026-10-11)

Ten lanes (five "fix first" votes) built online-only web apps and found that a
browser `createClient` refuses durable writes with `E_ADMISSION`, as does a
device-less `createApp`, so they shipped `webDevice()` and its wasm (2.1 MB,
647 KB gzip) with zero synced tables. Three lighter paths were assessed:

1. **A device-less `createApp` journaling through its online intent journal**
   (`app-online.ts`). That journal commits asynchronously through the session
   store's lock. A same-turn navigation after `mutate` returns could lose the
   click. Losing it never duplicates it (server id deduplication keeps
   at-most-once), but "a web client never loses a click" (§13.3; LLP 3000.007
   §20.4, W4a's synchronous journal and its navigation witness) is a stated,
   reviewed guarantee. A best-effort browser tier would be a new card word and
   needs the author's ruling.
2. **The synchronous localStorage journal without the interpreter.**
   `web-journal.ts` records synchronously, but its recovery admits records
   into the device's IndexedDB outbox under the authority stamp, Web Lock
   claims, orphan-tab adoption, store binding and session-epoch fences of §6.
   An online-only variant needs its own recovery, dispatch and cancellation
   through all of those: a new custody owner, not a contained change.
3. **Lazy-loading the wasm.** The device is the outbox and the admission
   authority and opens at sign-in; deferring its bytes defers custody, so an
