Both families reviewed the N1–N3 integration `fde962314` blind; each
re-check read only its own family's earlier output. The records are
`llp/reviews/3000.007-next-landing.*`.

| Round | Commit | GPT | Grok | Disposition |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `fde962314` | NOT READY: effects displaced row ids (1); presence-dependent refusals and meter cuts (2); the block wrapper bypassed population admission (3); short interrupted pages and lost siblings read complete (4); exact-bound scalar reads incomplete (5); the wrapper changed meters and sites (6) | READY WITH CHANGES: the same admission bypass (High); a short interrupted page read complete (Low); a two-block `where:1` charge (Low) | R1p (commit/ordinal effect ids, the totality rule, the untaken-arm charge, statement setup before admission; the lead mapped a meter cut after an untaken charge to a queued prediction) and R1g (per-page loss) |
| 2 | `33b530d41` | NOT READY: 1, 2, 3, 5 repaired; A (High) a repeated scan site erased an earlier loss; B (Medium) an auxiliary break poisoned an intact returned page; C (Medium) helper-return lowering still changed IR | READY | R2g (monotone loss, returned collectors only, a generated-shape oracle) and R2p (ownership in a binder side map; executed IR byte-identical to `ce15819ad` over 3,219 programs) |
| 3 | `4c1e825bc` | NOT READY: A, B, C repaired; D (High) a direct `return` from a page loop read complete; E (Medium) a discarded re-execution keeps its loss | three attempts exited without a review | The lead (`ba40649ef`): a return registers every enclosing loop and unvisited loops stay registered, red/green on the server and both stores; E accepted as conservative in §19.2. The three-round limit closes review here |

While the round-3 suite ran, `chat's real TypeScript invite worker is
supervised by dev` went red: an orphaned claim long-poll of a killed
worker could lease the next request to nobody. `dev` now gives each worker
child its own session, closed on exit (`0380b3ae6`, journal). The landing
merged `origin/main` (0.2.13, published by the performance program, and
the excellence program's prepared 0.2.14) and ships as 0.2.15.

## 20. Agent ergonomics: everything the Astra runs charged (2026-09-14)

The author set the goal on 2026-09-14: "solve every agent ergonomics problem
with snapback4 holding back the astra medium clique scores." An evidence
inventory of the 0.2.6, 0.2.9, 0.2.10 and 0.2.12 Astra lanes, the ceremony
bars and the September 5 competitor cells found the scorer grading defects
and misleading documentation, not features. Snapback 4 scored 87 on
setup_and_docs and 91 on diagnostics on 0.2.6; it scored 79 and 78 on 0.2.12,
charged for two defects the builder blamed on Snapback (§19.1, §19.2) and one
missing card. Each decision below anchors a lane of the next landings. The
inventory's identifiers (S01–S36) are cited per decision. Items on
`NOT-DOING.md` (ephemeral typing, relevance ranking) and items that would move
a ruling are not decisions here; they are questions for the author.

### 20.1 A word finds its card, and prediction has one (S01, S19, S20, S21, S04)

`snapback4 guide <word>` prints a card on stdout for every word a builder
reaches for. Aliases map to their card: `prediction`, `predict`, `offline`
and `optimistic` go to a new `prediction` card; `pagination` and `cursor` go
to `reads`; `migration` goes to schema evolution; `sql` goes to the inspection
verb; `push` and `notification` go to `effects`. A word with no card prints
the nearest cards on stdout and exits non-zero. The `prediction` card says
what makes a mutation predictable, with compiled examples:
- held, horizon and server sites, with `why <op>` and `check --residency`;
- a client-minted id already dedupes, so an `exists t[id]` guard past the
  horizon only costs prediction;
- `upsert` predicts an update and never an insert for a row the device lacks;
- presence decides only effects (§19.1).

Cards whose set-state recipes use `upsert` say how they predict. The writes
card carries a recipe for server-arrival order (a per-group ordinal kept by
the mutation). The README's sign-in section carries an onboarding recipe:
check handle availability by query, and treat a session with no profile as
onboarding.

**A card fits a tool window (wave 3 of the app farm, [LLP 3000.037](./3000.037-app-farm-new-project-friction.research.md); 2026-10-11).**
Forty lanes lost guide output to their tools' truncation, mostly by batching
several cards in one command. `guide <card>` prints a card whole only up to
130 lines (the start card's 124-line budget fits). A longer card prints its
opening, cut at a paragraph boundary after at most 40 lines, then a numbered
section index with line counts and the three ways to read more:
`--section <number or words>` (the index number; the heading in any case and
punctuation; a unique prefix; a substring; every word; a miss names the
nearest heading and the lines that mention the words), `--find <words>`
(matching lines with a line of context, under their section; the way into the
language card's 525-line Details block, which has no headings), and `--full`.
The rule is the same on a terminal and on a pipe, so the docs describe one
behavior; scripts that parse a card pass `--full`. Rejected: whole cards on a
TTY only (agents run under pipes, and the docs would describe two behaviors)
and a pager (no agent tool drives one). In the same wave, `clock`, `date`,
`duration` and `now` open a new short `time` card instead of the 386-line jobs
card; `guide cheatsheet` is one screen of the common forms around a compiled
schema; `guide api` indexes every package subpath, and a package test keeps it
equal to the exports; and `init` prints the files it wrote, since lanes
guessed `vite.config.ts` and `metro.config.cjs`.

**A topic word finds its section (wave 4 of the app farm, 0.4.19; 2026-10-11).**
Twenty lanes still lost time navigating: `--section` refused topic words
(`sync --section audience`, `client --section React`, `reads --section
Reference`) with exit 1 and a "nearest heading" chosen by spelling alone
(React → "Read boundaries"); five read a 21-line opening as the whole card
because the hint printed only below the index; and sections were coarse (the
rules card's "Reference" was 250 of 374 lines). Three changes:
- When no heading matches but the words occur, `--section` prints the section
  holding a majority of the lines that mention them (innermost heading, with a
  one-line note naming it and the `--find` command), or else the `--find`
  output when the mentions spread; both exit 0. Only words no line mentions
  exit 1, and only then is the nearest heading by spelling offered (a typo).
  `--find a|b` matches either alternative.
- The overview prints the hint as its second line, in the title's paragraph
  (`(This is the opening and section index of a N-line card: …)`), and keeps
  the "More:" line under the index. The title stays first and the lead stays
  the second paragraph, so tests and tools that read the lead keep working.
- Coarse sections gain `###` subsections that the index numbers: the rules
  card's Reference (hops, read through, Clique receipts, row rules, what a
  refused write returns, disclosure) and field authority (private fields), the
  sync card's Reference (audiences, horizons, acquisition, the wire, device
  versions; `sync --section audience` now prints 35 lines, not 271), and the
  types card's Details (column types, null guards, text bounds). Each card
  stays inside its line and word budgets by removing text it repeated or
  condensed legacy-compatibility detail (0.2.32/0.2.33). The
  language card's 470-line Details block is one compiled program run against
  the engine, so it stays whole; `--find` remains the way into it.

In the same wave about 25 "fix first" sections asked for one compiled
end-to-end shape rather than a feature, so `guide recipes` (aliases `roles`,
`admin`, `two-party`, `booking`, `capacity`, `reservation`, `recurring`, …;
`schedule` stays on `jobs`) carries four: roles (admin, staff, members, with
the first admin seeded or granted by a service seat), two parties (a buyer and
a seller, synced through a parties table), booking capacity (private bookings,
a public occupancy view, the duplicate checked before the seat count, `unique`
and `cap` as the backstop) and schedules (decide by `now` where possible; a
look-back sweep that catches up after coalesced boundaries). The suite runs
each recipe's `test.cases.jsonl` lines against its schema with `test`.

**Words, parts and one refusal story (wave 5 of the app farm, 0.4.20; 2026-10-11).**
Fifteen lanes still lost time navigating, and the long tail asked for about
fifteen one-line answers no card gave. Changes:
- `--find a b` prints the lines holding every word, each as written or
  singular (`loops` finds "loop"); `a|b` and `a OR b` (043 wrote it) are
  either. When no line holds them all (010's `enum time principal`), the
  lines holding any of them print under a note saying so, and the exit stays
  1, the miss signal scripts and the suite already read. Unquoted words after
  `--find`/`--section` continue the search instead of being dropped. A single
  match reads "1 line mentions".
- The language card's program prints in twelve parts under `###` headings
  inside Details (tables and rules; messages; public tables; views; helpers;
  queries; loops, conditionals, arithmetic; text and search; mutations; jobs;
  calendar windows; planned reads), so `--section loops` (028) works.
  `guide::language()` concatenates the parts back into the one program the
  suite runs against the engine; test contexts and the readauth census treat
  each part as that program. This reverses wave 4's "stays whole": the
  program is still one program, only printed in parts. The card stays within
  its 825-line limit (blank lines between declarations inside a part were
  dropped) and within the six reference cards' shared word target (the reads
  card drops a dated latency measurement, the writes card a harness
  description and one regression's numbers).
- Aliases builders tried: `query`/`queries` → reads (070), `loop`/`loops` →
  language, `insert`/`update`/`upsert`/`delete` → writes, `division`/`integer`
  → types, `reserved` → cheatsheet.
- `guide refusals` step 3 said an update or delete of an unreadable row is
  `NOT_FOUND` before the write rule runs, contradicting the same card's
  delete-by-id paragraph; the engine (`write.rs` `delete_attempt`,
  `update_attempt`) judges the write rule first and answers `NOT_FOUND` only
  when it refuses a hidden row (`E_RULE` on a readable one), except that a
  table with `read through` children needs the row readable. Step 3 and
  `guide testing` now say that; and `test` no longer attributes such a
  `NOT_FOUND` to "the program's own refusal at removeSale:2" (041, 061): it
  quotes the write's source line and names the write target.
- One-line answers, each checked against the binary first: text escapes,
  integer `/` and `%` (Euclidean floor; money and decimal do not divide), no
  `int` range form, `last` reads newest first, how bracket keys bind,
  renaming in a projection, absent `delete` and its idempotent guard,
  per-statement `unique`, a parent delete leaving referencing rows, the full
  reserved-word lists (cheatsheet); a sweep reading a second table (jobs); view
  clause order and online-only sources (totals); a job or query at `/m/` is
  400 `E_OP` (wire); the staff grant admits admins (recipes).

**The owner-or-staff page before the note (wave 6 of the app farm, 0.4.21;
2026-10-11).** 21 lanes (43 minutes, nine "fix first" votes) applied
`N_NEVER_COMPLETE`'s branched rewrite and asked for it to appear before the
note: `guide recipes` showed a staff-only `queue` (with `require`) and an
owner-only `mine`, never the one page both read. Now the recipes card's
opening example and its Roles recipe carry `board`, `if exists
staff[viewer]:` returning the whole page and otherwise `return … where
.author = viewer …`, with two `test.cases.jsonl` lines (staff `complete`,
a member `complete`) that the suite runs against the recipe's schema; the
Roles prose says why one `or` scan cannot promise completeness and two
queries split the screen. The cheatsheet's schema gains an owner-or-staff
`requests` table (`online only`, the comment naming the two-audience sync
limit) and the same `board`, staying at 130 lines (it still prints whole)
by merging blank lines and short bullets. `guide start` keeps its 124-line
budget: its prelude names the form in one sentence and points to the
compiled versions. The cheatsheet's `if exists t[id]: delete t[id]`
one-liner was not Quarry (the parser refuses a statement after `:` on the
same line); it now says to put the `delete` on the next line.

### 20.2 The CLI and client stop inviting mistakes (S02, S03, S22, S28, S32)

- **Assets:** the README's React asset example narrows `status` and renders
  the image, and typechecks.
- **Sign-out:** the `Client` type a builder holds exposes sign-out, or the
  README names the type that does.
- **init:** `init --online`/`--expo` merges into an existing `package.json`
  instead of refusing it.
- **Replayed writes:** a replayed write's result is typed as absent,
  following `issues/20260914-snapback4-write-result-type-omits-replay-state.md`.
- **Replay flags:** `dev --replay` suppresses new effects and holds schedule
  admission without app code (W5a, 2026-09-15; calibration G2). Emission keeps
  its evaluation and meter; a successful mutation or job chunk increments a
  durable suppression count in the same transaction instead of storing an
  effect payload. Refusals and duplicate mutations add no count. `doctor`
  reports `suppressed`; restarting with or without replay never delivers
  these effects. The dev store retains the policy for local `run` until the
  next host start, which sets it from its flags; a normal start clears the
  policy and keeps the count. Replay skips held schedule periods on release
  and already queued jobs still run. Existing effects keep their ordinary
  lifecycle. `--hold-effects` only pauses claims and keeps effects claimable
  later; `--hold-schedules` only holds admission. `--replay` is one spelling
  for the no-notifications replay task, rather than a second independent
  suppression flag. It is refused outside `dev` or with `--release`
  (`E_REPLAY_DEV_ONLY`); production always emits normally.
- **Expo:** `init --expo` writes the Metro configuration the web device's wasm
  needs.

**2026-10-07 — DK rounds 1–2: refused bearers explain themselves within the dev trust boundary.**
The authority decision and `E_AUTH`/`auth` envelope stay unchanged. Detailed
wording requires both dev mode and the same loopback peer/Host/Origin check as
dev-only endpoints. Declared public POST routes bypass dev admission, so they
must explicitly apply that check before choosing an explanation. Serve and
untrusted dev requests use identical text for all token states: "this session
is not live; sign in again". This avoids an issued-token membership oracle.
No reason field, store identity, token or principal is added to the refusal.

After authority refuses, a read-only lookup may identify expiry from an existing
full/read-session record. A refused unexpired record can explain loss of authority.
Absent records remain ambiguous: a token may come from an earlier or replaced
store or another instance, or have expired or been signed out, including before
this server started. The repair is sign in again and discard saved tokens from
an earlier store. No token history or process cache is kept, no store format
changes, and diagnostics add or remove nothing at store open. Detached auth/poll
readers keep their existing admission ordering; lookup cannot change authority.

Identity doors (`logout`, `narrow`, `refresh`, `logout-all`) preserve the same
`Refusal` as query/schema/changes/actions: HTTP 401 for a terminal refused bearer,
`E_AUTH`/`auth`, the unprefixed message and `guide: personas`. A retryable refusal
keeps HTTP 503. Logout and narrowing still authorize inside their writer
transaction; only after a refusal does the HTTP adapter choose diagnostic prose.
A live credential of the wrong kind keeps the operation's own explanation.
Refresh losing authority between initial resolution and rotation also preserves
the envelope; it never wraps the sentence in `RuntimeError::Auth`.

SDK online/local terminal cleanup retains the validated refusal instead of
synthesizing "sign in to continue"; app fences and the online arm preserve it too.
A terminal E_AUTH during device-app restoration also enters the signed-out
facade when no valid previous owner is being restored: `app.ready`, `app.auth.why`
and `app.online` query/mutate/act retain the same explanation. Local `logoutAll`
keeps a cause already retained after session death. Successful sign-in replaces
that cause; never-signed-in clients stay generic. The first current-credential
refusal wins; obsolete rotation refusals and retryable auth failures retain their
existing rules. Ordinary signed-out clients still ask
for sign-in. No new public field or generated API shape is required; package
declaration generation checks the existing contract.

### 20.3 A Following feed that is complete and cheap is on the card (S14, S15)

Every Astra run rebuilt Following differently, and the 0.2.12 grader found
its read-time filter returning short incomplete pages at scale. The feeds
card carries one paved Following feed. It is complete at the scale envelope
(1,000 users, a 500-follow reader, sparse readers) and answers on the device.
Following a user acquires that author's recent posts; unfollowing removes
them; reposts and the reader's own posts appear. `check` notes a `where`
filter whose predicate pins nothing in the scanned index prefix, because at
scale such a filter returns short incomplete pages, and the rewrite names the
recipe. The lane records the design it chose, and the alternatives it
measured, in this section.


**Built by lane C, 2026-09-14: choose the hybrid.** The simulator seeds
1,000 author identities, exactly 50,000 source events and 1,415 follow
edges: independent 0/1/5/500-follow readers, a celebrity with 900 followers
and 200 posts, a celebrity-plus-four reader, and a five-follower writer.
All three candidates run in the same interpreter with the default meters.
Each latency is the nearest-rank p95 of 20 samples after three warm-ups,
in milliseconds on the shared development host; these are simulator
observations, not HTTP or competitor claims. Cold rows come from actual
partition snapshots. Index entries are the existing `Metered.index_entries`
counter (plain row scans charge `examined`, hence zero in the read column).
The comparison is an explicitly run ignored measurement test; the selected
recipe's envelope and both-store device tests run in the blocking suite.
Bulk fixture loading removes caps only during seed acquisition, then adopts
the original schema to validate every row, unique index and cap before any
query, write or snapshot is measured.

The old unscoped filter returns 4/20 and 8/20 for the zero- and one-follow
readers, both `complete: false` at 8,193 examined (the attempted charge
that crosses the 8,192 ceiling). The five-follow case fills 20 only after
7,969 examined. The merge fills every page but visits up to 501 lanes and
costs 12.60 times the five-follow read in this run. Full fan-out reads one
prefix but its celebrity acknowledgement costs 79.63 times the
five-follower acknowledgement. The hybrid has one private lane plus one
lane per pulled author: 22 examined without a celebrity, 45 with one,
and two writes for a celebrity post. The first hybrid latency sample set
contains host-load outliers (the identical 22-row one-follow read took
3.775 ms); its celebrity read exceeded the 3× ratio and is repeated alone
below rather than counted as passing on that sample.

The isolated hybrid repeat (`SB4_FEED_CANDIDATE=hybrid cargo test -p
snapback4-sim --test clique following_candidates_at_scale -- --ignored
--nocapture`) measured read p95s of **0.364 / 0.343 / 0.356 / 0.373 /
0.577 ms** for 0 / 1 / 5 / 500 / celebrity-plus-four follows. Ordinary and
celebrity acknowledgement p95s were **1.664 / 0.637 ms**. The dense/5-follow,
celebrity/5-follow and celebrity/ordinary-write ratios were **1.05× / 1.62× /
0.38×**, all below 3×. Every read again filled 20, was complete, and had
identical deterministic meter counts to the table. The noisy first sample
is retained above; the deterministic counts and both-store correctness
assertions, not a wall-clock threshold on a shared host, are the regressions.

The recipe promotes an account permanently on its 51st follower, adding
pull rows for its current followers and itself in that same transaction.
Each event's delivery mode is immutable: earlier events remain pushed and
future events broadcast, so promotion creates no duplicate. Follow copies
the newest `authors.max(200).min(917)` source events only when they were pushed
(§20.19: sized with the caps in wave 10, then bounded by the 1,024-row mutation
write ceiling less a 107-row promotion allowance); shared events are
read directly. Unfollow deletes all private rows by that actor and its pull
row atomically; the viewer's own original and repost remain. Backfill of
200 rows measured 207 examined / 1,405 index entries / 201 written; the
matching purge measured 204 / 1,003 / 201. Repeating follow, unfollow or
repost inserts nothing twice. The 220-post lifecycle case checks the exact
backfill boundary and pagination across promotion, unfollow and refollow.

Two small additions make this possible without changing audiences or
horizon semantics. A merge lane may name a second table with the header's
columns and the same plain index; each scan still uses that table's own
rule and residency. The first lane owns the existing cursor descriptor;
the interpreter validates it before discovery and translates it for the
other table. Serialized values, IR variants and cursor encodings do not
change. IDs identify an item across projections; copies keep their
ordering fields consistent. `cap N` with no `by` uses the existing cap's
empty prefix to bound an entire table. Both forms are on the language
card, and positive/refusal regressions were red against the pre-change
implementation at `33b530d41b00f1d685656f360e37c52ec1255ad6` before passing.

**2026-09-14 — review round 1, lane W2R1m:** the shared cursor is withheld
when a merge encounters a non-uniform read, a meter cut or a word-limit
cut. An unfinished lane may still contain a readable row ahead of the
last returned key; advancing every lane to that key would skip it. The
non-uniform class withholds `next` even within budget, so hidden rows
cannot change cursor presence by exhausting the meter. Uniform merges
within budget keep their existing pagination, including equal ordering
keys and projection deduplication. This applies to ordinary, cross-table
and matching merges on every host; no serialized cursor form changes.
Merged cursors bind the table, index, direction and typed ordering suffix, not
the generation: a matching descriptor continues through the current data
after adoption. The feeds card states that contract.
**2026-09-17 — wave 13, lane W13a (LLP 3000.007.000):** the meter-cut arm gains
one exception — a cut while *draining* a uniform lazy merge, every head known,
records `next` after its last emitted row; an opening cut, a word cut and the
non-uniform class stay withheld, and the class is now applied when the outcome
is built, so the rule holds in both statement orders. The merged position
carries the row id when the suffix lacks it; the serialized v1 form is
unchanged, and a token minted for a position without the id is refused.
§20.22.5.
Direct table and maintain page cursors bind the evaluated prefix and active
generation under §20.9; their tokens are refused after adoption.

Private inboxes and public broadcasts sync in full under declared caps:
50,000 private rows per reader, 32,000 broadcasts total, 1,000 source events
per actor, 1,000 follows per account and 32 pulled authors per reader.
This avoids the exhausted-horizon ambiguity even for an empty lane. Caps
refuse an over-limit write atomically; archiving or a larger application
design is required beyond them. The public broadcast projection reaches
every device (200 rows in this envelope); raw posts and the follow graph
stay online. This makes no subset-public-sync or union-audience claim.
The rejected private-group prototype stopped at the existing grant guard;
that authorization rule is unchanged. There is no job or exact horizon
maintenance. This replaces the chronological Following recipe described
by LLP 3000.004; that document's ranked-feed recipe remains unchanged.

`N_SPARSE_FILTER` is limited to row-dependent, unscoped paged query scans
without a seek or matching prefix, whose predicate pins no leading index
column. In an `or`, both branches must pin that column to avoid the note;
a scoped prefix or seek avoids it. Its rewrite names the feeds card.
The card and README compile without a diagnostic or note. Both device
stores match server data and cursor pages at the envelope, and stream the
follow-time backfill and unfollow purge. Dense acquisition of 25,250 rows
measured 3,130.977 ms on SQLite and 2,826.078 ms on memory, after a
765.905 ms server snapshot; those wall times include the device apply calls.

**2026-09-15 — W7a: installed authority and synchronous prediction.**
The 0.2.22 calibration exposed a ghost source reference through the prefixed
recipe's standalone `feedCreatePost`. A prefixed install now converts every
standalone mutation into a `fn`; the app owns all client mutations and validates
or creates its post before inserting a reference event. Only Following remains
a client query, and the purge remains a system job. Unprefixed standalone
reference-event programs retain their operations.

Restoring synchronous offline profile save, post creation and follow backfill
requires more than syncing author modes: the follow graph and source references
are read by those helpers too. The recipe syncs these already-public rows and
makes pull routing public, derived from the public graph. Global caps bound
this metadata to 1,000 authors, 100,000 edges, 60,000 source references and
32,000 pull routes; the existing per-account and engine meter ceilings remain.
Private inboxes retain their complete capped partitions. Copy inserts rely on
a fresh event or a new follow rather than an `if absent` probe into another
reader's private inbox. Predicting loops cover the declared group cap; the
backfill stops after the newest `authors.max(200).min(917)` events — a fixed 200
until wave 10 sized it with the caps, and bounded since by the mutation write
ceiling so a follow cannot refuse `E_BOUND` inside the declared envelope (§20.19).

This pays acquisition for synchronous prediction: the wired 500-follow witness
acquires **3,095 rows / 335,403 JSON payload bytes**, previously 1,055 rows.
The 50,000-event recipe envelope acquires **78,566 rows**, including 25,050
private entries, for 500 follows. The card publishes the measured table counts;
this change makes no cold-start reduction claim. Following remains 20 complete
entries with 82 examinations and 21 probes in the wired 5/500 witness.

**2026-09-16 — W11a, promotion preserves every existing delivery (author's lane brief).**
This changes W7a's intentional policy of skipping saturated followers. Promotion
requires successful route installation for every follower, including the triggering
reader; a follower at 32 pulls refuses the entire follow/promotion transaction with
`FEED_PROMOTION_PULL_CAP`. App and recipe edges, author mode, routes and counts roll
back together, leaving existing pushed delivery intact. Show the refusal; each
saturated follower must unfollow a shared author to free a slot before retrying the
refused follow with a new write ID. If they cannot, decline the new follow and keep
pushed delivery. More than 32 shared authors needs a separate serving design, not a
cap increase. A new follow of an already-shared author without a slot still refuses
`FEED_PULL_CAP`. Requiring route success adds no writes: the 107-write promotion
allowance and 917-event maximum backfill stay unchanged.
A saturated author's own shared events get an own-inbox copy. Edges record
`at: now`, with `0` as the default for imported edges of unknown age.

### 20.4 A queued web write survives navigation (S29)

**2026-09-29 — EA round 3, wait before admission.** The supervisor withdrew
rounds 0–2's durable pre-identity design. Three review rounds found new handoff
defects at native owners, orphan transfer, restore and the online journal. The
ordinary first-save path was sound; calibration #26 d-01 needs the early call to
wait, not a second durable queue. This decision replaces all three EA amendments
previously here; their reports and commits retain the evidence.

A mutation on a session-ready but unidentified replica allows **15 seconds of
identity I/O from the call**, inside `mutate()`. Only time waiting behind an
earlier ordinary admission is excluded. Waiting behind a predecessor's identity
checks still consumes the budget; a burst cannot multiply the 15-second wait
when no admission has begun. The final identity recheck uses the remaining budget, with the deadline checked again after I/O completes. Its promise stays pending, including with
`waitSeconds: 0`. `usePendingWrites()` and `write(id)` expose runtime-only pending
state with “waiting for backend identification; not yet admitted”. No intent,
row IDs, prediction, receipt or deadline is persisted before identity. Reload or
close loses this unadmitted call; it was never acknowledged as queued. Closing
settles a live caller with `E_CLOSED`. Applications should preserve an editable
draft while submission is in flight. Timers resume on a suspended runtime's next
turn; a late identification is rejected against the original deadline.

Once identified, calls from that client enter ordinary admission in call order.
The wait lane releases at admission, without waiting for server settlement.
A published store ID is ready only when backend adoption is no longer required,
including at opening and after sync observations/publication. Temporary unreadiness
at the final check continues polling within the same remaining budget. A native
admission rechecks the adoption flag under its writer lock, closing the gap after
the SDK read; the browser admission plan already applies that fence.
Ordinary prediction eligibility, authorization, stable IDs, input deduplication,
localStorage/IndexedDB or SQLite custody and outbox delivery then apply unchanged.
The online app likewise waits before writing new intent into its journal;
recovery of already admitted ordinary intent retains its existing behavior.
There is no cross-owner ordering promise for calls that have not been admitted.

The captured schema generation and authenticated `/schema` store identity fence
adoption, reset and incarnation replacement during the wait. Each call pins its
store identity and backend fingerprint at its first successful identification,
including when the cached backend has no store ID. Backend contents compare
with stable object-key ordering and programs sorted by name, using the common
interpreter fields (`name`, `kind`, `args`, `body`, `native`,
`read_time_granularity_ms`, `returned_shapes`). Ordered program bodies remain
ordered. Filling a missing server-only native descriptor or execution metadata
from `/schema` after an offline open does not change this identity; schema or
interpreter-program changes still do. Store, generation and pinned device
fingerprint checks remain independent. Every subsequent check and
the ordinary admission request use those pins; later observations cannot
retarget a call while it waits behind an earlier admission. Revalidation at the
ordinary admission boundary covers a change between the check and commit. Both
browser adapters forward the generation and backend pins into the serialized
journal plan, which compares them with current device metadata before allocating
a submission or invoking admission. Synchronous capture alone cannot fence an
adoption already queued ahead of that transaction. An incompatible store or failed final identity read returns `E_ADMISSION_STORE`;
identity I/O exceeding its budget returns `E_ADMISSION_TIMEOUT`. Both reach the
public refusal callback, lookup and `onWrite`; raw device errors do not escape. Both are public, actionable, unsent refusals.
`onWrite` reports the refusal; a new attempt on the same mounted form works after
repair. Neither timeout nor close expires an admitted write. An ordinary
`E_ADMISSION` storage refusal after waiting releases the unadmitted ID reservation
just as the synchronous refusal does, so repairing storage permits the documented
same-ID retry. Exact-input comparison still applies to admitted or running calls.

The 15-second choice gives ten times calibration #26's measured 1.5-second
settling interval. Round-3 controlled fresh-client measurements additionally
record the interval from releasing startup to first settlement on process, wasm,
Worker and online hosts, plus real deadline measurements. It is an interactive
submission bound, not a network or whole-acquisition performance guarantee.

Removed: deferred metadata and its native compare/binding/FIFO protocol,
publication timestamps and freeze saves, deferred orphan adoption, online
pre-identity journal capture/deadlines/dispatch claims, and their handoff-only
tests/model schedules. Preserved: ordinary outbox and recovery, public refusal
cards, first-save regressions adapted to pending promises, schema-store fencing,
and the ordinary close-receipt and explicit-sync follow-up fixes with tests.
The original I1–I13 session model remains; wait-specific schedules are separate.

The calibration narrative called the form permanently stuck, but its trace and
the controlled mounted-form test show refusals until identity and success after
identity without remount. This change makes the first call wait automatically.
Evidence: `snapback4/reports/20260929-ea-admit-before-identity/round3/`.

On the web, admission waits for the outbox's IndexedDB commit. `pagehide`
or becoming hidden sends the oldest durable unconfirmed write with an
authenticated keepalive request, including a retry of that same head when
an ordinary send is in flight. A blocked or oversized head is never skipped;
requests across clients share the browser's **64 KiB body budget**. Unsent
or unconfirmed writes stay durable for retry on reopen with the same mutation
ID, so replay cannot apply a write twice. If the exit response has not finished
after **one second**, ordinary flushing retries the same durable head before
advancing. `close()` stops waiting immediately without cancelling keepalive.

Admission that finishes while the page is suspended rechecks exit transport
after its commit. Exit notifications wait for the local session-lock queue
to drain, including a turn queued after admission; notification itself holds
no session lock, so peer logout and transport's authority checks can proceed.
On reopen, a matching server store identity and
non-regressed head allow unknown writes to replay before the first sync
finishes; §18.2's replacement and restore rules still apply.

**2026-09-15 — W4a, synchronous pre-admission journal.** Before `mutate`
returns its promise, a web host holding its exclusive persistence claim captures the
mutation id, operation, arguments, minted row ids and submission order in
localStorage. That synchronous store survives same-origin navigation; no network request exposes an unadmitted write.
On open, its records enter the existing IDB outbox in order before new writes.
A failed admission save leaves the record recoverable before a surviving page's
next admission too. A closed tab's records use the same exclusive claim and orphan
adoption rule: the next device opening the store adopts them, never a live tab's.
Recovery and ordinary admission allocate queued submission numbers from the same
device counter in the serialized host chain, including recovery deferred until
backend adoption. Capture order also advances past the journal already held.
Already-queued primary writes precede recovered orphan records.

Under the orphan's lock, a matching healthy destination installs its authenticated
backend before recovering records left behind `backend_required`. An orphan with
no kept backend or store identity is skipped, leaving its journal intact for a
later matching open; no identity is guessed from its journal key. Malformed or
unusable orphans are isolated so healthy stores still open, and one malformed
journal key cannot hide other tabs. A failed destination commit still discards
its uncommitted VM. Skipping neither loses a record nor makes it executable: the
usual identity fence and transfer acknowledgement must succeed on a later open.

An IDB transfer marker shares the admission transaction and suppresses duplicate
admission by mutation id against queued writes and receipts, including after a
receipt leaves the outbox while localStorage removal is failing. It contains no
server result or terminal settlement. Successful transfer removes the synchronous
record; acknowledged markers are collected when that removal succeeds. A
live admission's prediction or validation refusal keeps the ordinary failed outcome
even if bookkeeping fails. It removes the journal record, replaces it with a
non-executable cancellation, or acknowledges it in IDB. If neither store can
persist cancellation, recovery is indeterminate: an executable record may remain
and later be admitted if the authored condition changes. A returned refusal does
not promise preserved cancellation when both stores fail. Original arguments
and minted ids survive recovery. Sends remain exclusively the outbox's, in its existing order, with the
original mutation id; there is no new exit ordering or settlement path.

Recovered, previously unadmitted records keep their source backend store identity
until they leave the outbox. An identity mismatch retires them without sending
them to the replacement, including after an offline reopen and orphan adoption.
This is stricter than §18.2's treatment of ordinary already-admitted unknown
writes, which is unchanged. Same-store restore refusal still halts sending.

The journal is bounded to **32 records and 256 KiB** of UTF-8 keys and values
per device store, and **64 KiB per serialized record**. Unavailable, throwing or
full localStorage, exceeded bounds, or
browser storage clearing leave that write's unawaited navigation **best-effort**:
the write can still be lost before IDB commits. A journal-only write needs another client to
open before it can be admitted and sent. Keepalive remains best-effort and sends
only admitted writes. These are navigation/reopen guarantees, not a claim about
physical power loss. Built-in IndexedDB now refuses opening without Web Locks.
Custom providers must supply an exclusive claim; alternate names must use the
requested store's `:tab-` namespace and support discovery/removal so closed
stores can be adopted. Non-alternate claims must name the exact requested store. For programmatic
navigation, `await client.mutate(...)` remains the strongest durable boundary; handle `failed` before leaving.
`pending` means IDB admission is durable and the server outcome is unconfirmed.
The writes card and README state these limits.

**2026-09-16 recovery correction.** A surviving executable journal record is
an indeterminate intent. Recovery uses the existing replay-candidate admission
path: successful local prediction is retained, but a local refusal becomes an
unpredicted queued entry whose outcome the server decides. Stale rows in either
the primary or an orphan cannot permanently cancel it before catching up.
Live admission still returns its ordinary refusal and attempts cancellation;
already transferred/cancelled records are skipped before recovery. Store binding,
original IDs, durable FIFO and replacement fences remain unchanged. This needs
no new device wire operation or cross-platform host callback.

The Node model covers same-turn teardown and an unresolved admission save, one
and two writes, original row ids, order and at-most-once application, stale
journals with queued and retired receipts, refusal, storage failure and bounds,
closed/live tabs, and store replacement. W4R1a adds deferred backend recovery
followed by an offline successor (ABC), backend-required and unusable orphans,
independent cancellation-store failures, absent Web Locks, malformed-key
discovery, queued-primary-before-orphan order, and an unidentified backend.
The lead's real Chromium run of
`witness/navigation-immediate.mjs` (chromium-1243, outside the sandbox) passes
**10 of 10**, against the **8 of 10** residual at 0.2.19 recorded in §20.12;
both unawaited zero-delay cases apply exactly once.

**2026-09-16 — W11R1a, terminal receipts have shared custody.** Before an
adopted tab store can be removed, its value-free terminal write history is
committed to `${name}:receipts`, where `name` already binds server and viewer.
A separate, nonwaiting Web Lock serializes merges into one record bounded by
`WRITE_HISTORY_LIMIT` (256); existing shared ids keep their outcome and position,
and new recovered ids append in recovery order. Every opener and receipt lookup
reads that window alongside its own device window without copying or refreshing
it. The shared record contains no pending state, outbox, arguments or results.
A failed shared commit leaves the source intact. Winning adoption therefore
cannot move a terminal receipt out of reach of a replacement tab; ordinary
bounded eviction and browser storage loss remain possible.

A held store lock remains the ownership authority; there is no reliable separate
live/dead signal. Adoption takes one nonwaiting attempt per candidate per pass,
with no foreground retry sleep. **2026-09-16 — W11R2:** busy candidates now use
one cancellable queued Web Lock request per lock as a release signal, replacing
the one-second background poll. Recovery rechecks current stores after the lock
releases; a live or suspended owner's lock is never stolen. Unidentified or
structurally unresolved journals wait for an open or identity/sync signal, and
persistence failures get at most three retries after 1, 2 and 4 seconds per open.
Receipt lookups first test whether the shared window exists and never create it.
Closing cancels waits and retry, and an adopted outbox wakes ordinary client
flushing even when no backend change arrives. Deterministic tests force A to remove B before C
opens, hold a candidate past the completed foreground open, and exercise sent
and failed receipts, exclusive queued writes, failed shared persistence,
concurrent adopters, immutable duplicates and the 256-entry bound.

**2026-09-28 — Worker execution and page authority (SS rounds 4–5).**
The journal now separates its page-local capture, authority and cleanup from
VM execution. The same admission, exit-recovery and binding plans have
synchronous and asynchronous executors; original ids, captured order, arguments,
minted ids and authority remain in the page's record. The existing default
opener retains synchronous admission and exit dispatch.

The internal Worker host runs the unchanged wasm and strict IndexedDB
adapter together. Each private call must commit before its result can return;
the `j` transfer marker and outbox change share that transaction. Rows, staged
images and full persistence deltas stay in the Worker. Round 4 introduced that
foundation; round 5 integrates the public opt-in described below.

The page retains the exclusive store claim. Before any persistence, the Worker
acknowledges a second lifetime Web Lock named for that claimed store. A
replacement Worker page uses the same lifetime name, so navigation cannot race an old
Worker that has not stopped yet. On failure or explicit termination the page
waits for that lifetime lock, then an IndexedDB read transaction behind prior
writes, before restoring from durable state. Close after termination also
restores under the claim before releasing ownership. A failed barrier remains
sticky; a later close cannot forget it and release the claim.
`terminate()` itself is not a persistence acknowledgement. A lost reply after
commit rejects the call; journal replay discovers its durable marker instead
of admitting the same id again.

Chromium qualification and remaining work are in
[SS round 4](../snapback4/reports/20260927-ss-sync-scale/ROUND4.md).
SS round 5 adds a control snapshot after strict durability: store/generation,
acquisition incarnation, prediction tables (unknown blocks), queue revision,
issued-time floor and restore/send fences. Synchronous journal capture fences
page reads before transfer; only that id's committed acknowledgement releases
it. An older Worker reply cannot clear a newer capture. The local query path
can use this internal capability for already server-answered cold watches;
held reads, composition and supplementary delivery collection stay disabled
on that bypass. Store/head, credentials, expiry and final-publication fences
still apply. The ordinary opener supplies no such capability and is unchanged.

The internal suspension helper durably prepares the bound oldest head's
`begin_send` before giving the page dispatch permission. Every subsequent
transaction invalidates that permission synchronously at enqueue, including
`sync_state`; old network captures retain the preceding send revision and
are refused. Dispatch checks this permission and the page control snapshot,
then captures the exit journal synchronously before keepalive. If preparation
is stale or capture fails, the head stays durable for ordinary recovery.
Preparation runs on outbox changes, not after every sync capture. The public
adapter integrates this helper; a busy pagehide with stale preparation retains
its durable head for recovery instead of dispatching it.

The internal adapter also recovers orphan journals under the orphan's page
claim and Worker lifetime lock, transfers queued custody once, and commits
shared terminal receipts before deleting the source. Full row images stay
inside the source Worker. Delivery's conditional CAS transfers only its
`device:delivery:` metadata delta to the page; the existing strict IDB
transaction checks the page's `current()` callback immediately before commit.
Abort discards the Worker VM and restores from durability before reuse. No
callback is cloned and no earlier page check substitutes for that commit.

The opt-in is now `webDevice({ worker: true })`, with the ordinary host still
the default. Both openers wait for a preceding Worker's lifetime and IDB
barrier after taking the page claim, including mixed navigation. The packaged
entry supports the default offline wasm cache and supplied URLs, bytes,
Response promises and compiled modules. Injected persistence providers stay
on the ordinary host; `worker:true` with `persist` explicitly refuses rather
than cloning callbacks or silently moving that provider to another realm.
An empty offline open checks only backend metadata under the exclusive,
quiescent claim, avoiding a failed VM startup before first installation. A
temporary control barrier keeps cold-watch eligibility but sets prediction
authority to unknown: it withholds delivery without queuing a local read.
Round 5's repeated Chromium measurements establish responsive 1,000-conversation
watches, but acquisition still exceeds the 27 s target and the 100-conversation
control. No guide recommendation or landing qualification follows from these
tests. Measurements, failures and outstanding review are in
[SS round 5](../snapback4/reports/20260927-ss-sync-scale/ROUND5.md).

**2026-09-28 — SS round 6, real-app acquisition.** The Clique web export
and copied full-scale store are now the measurement workload; the largest
account is selected from actual memberships. IndexedDB publication keeps
the existing bucket format and strict transaction. A pure deletion delta
may replace per-row overflow deletes with a range delete only after a read
in that transaction proves every existing physical key belongs to the
deletion set. The read stops at the number of unique requested deletions
plus one; an unrelated survivor, a mixed put/delete delta or an incomplete
proof keeps individual deletes. Packed bucket contents are still updated
individually. Pure bucket deletions need no insertion-capacity calculation,
so removed images are not re-encoded to measure their old size. Row images,
watermark, outbox and staging changes retain one abort/commit boundary.
The wasm ABI, index implementation and budget are unchanged; a measured
sorted bulk-index candidate exceeded the budget and was discarded.
The sync card explains per-group multiplication and public inherited
interaction views; `N_MAINTAIN_SYNCED` already names Clique's two views.
Measurements, rejected candidates and remaining review requirements are in
[SS round 6](../snapback4/reports/20260927-ss-sync-scale/ROUND6.md).

**2026-09-29 — AQ, bounded adaptive browser buckets.** Cold acquisition on
the retained PF/SQ scale store spends most of its wall time in strict IndexedDB
saves. Grouping 256 reads into one request did not improve the measured wall
time. Reducing the initial physical bucket count did; keeping that reduction
fixed would spill a heavy partition too early.

Format 3 therefore begins each row namespace with 64 roots. A root that would
exceed the existing **512-entry / 256 KiB UTF-8** cap splits once into four
leaves, using the next two bits of the same hash. Each leaf keeps those caps
and the existing sticky per-row overflow rule. The directory has a fixed maximum
of 64 roots and 256 leaves per namespace. An ordinary update reads its root
and, only if split, its addressed leaf; it does not scan another bucket or the
overflow. The one-time split redistributes at most the capped old root plus
the caller's delta. It never changes logical rows, indexes or acquisition facts.

Every root, leaf, overflow, metadata and outbox change remains in one strict
transaction. Conditional saves check their predicate after all root/child
callbacks issue their writes, then commit in that same callback turn. A failed
save discards the host VM as before; progress still follows durable page apply.
The proved deletion-range optimization remains unchanged. Empty split roots
remain routing records and contain no logical row images.

Opening format 1 or 2 repartitions packed and overflow rows together in one
strict transaction, retaining metadata, outbox and staged acquisition. Removing
the old overflow entries is essential: otherwise a stale direct row can shadow
a packed update. An abort leaves the complete old row format usable by the
current adapter, including point reads before migration. Legacy stores without a bucket-format marker
remain per-row stores. The wasm, wire, schema, authorization, coverage, meters
and public client contract do not change.

**AQ round 1 — fence cached older clients.** Format 3 opens at physical
IndexedDB database version **2**, up from 1. The version-change transaction
preserves every existing object store and marker; only a new database creates
the `changes` store. Bucket migration still runs separately with strict
durability. Even if it aborts, the version fence stays installed and the current
adapter can retry. Old clients calling `open(name, 1)` reject with the browser's
`VersionError` before loading or saving: they cannot misinterpret format 3 as
an unpacked store, resurrect deletes or shadow packed updates with direct rows.
An exclusive ownership lock alone cannot protect sequential incompatible owners.
The sync guide explains reloading updated page/Worker bundles, including their
offline availability; discarding the store is not the upgrade procedure.
The Chromium regression runs the actual pre-AQ adapter from `f9620c815` beside
the current one with 600 rows, metadata, outbox, stage and base images; it
checks downgrade refusals and preserved contents, plus new-store fencing.
The abort/retry regression asserts `durability === "strict"` on both migration
transactions. These are browser transaction/version witnesses, not physical
power-loss measurements.
Grok's additional coverage finding adds packed and overflow prediction-base
images (`b`) to the abort/retry fixture, with point reads after migration and
after updating overflow. Removing `b` from packing is rejected by that test.
Format-1 bounds are checked on every physical bucket, including leaves, and
the split test checks every key against a distinct original value.

The browser regression pins 64 bucket reads/writes and one strict transaction
for a 10,000-row batch, split/conditional-save rollback, migration rollback and
overflow replacement, plus complete offline reopening after a multi-page
12,000-row acquisition on both devices. The retained-fixture witness compares
every stored row with the server's snapshot/catch-up pages. Measurements and
limits: [AQ round 0](../snapback4/reports/20260929-aq-fast-acquisition/REPORT.md).

**2026-09-28 — SS round 7, restore evidence and completed admissions.**
A cold query's valid same-store head below its captured published/private/image
floor is restore evidence, even if its read has since been fenced by an admission.
It immediately withdraws that incarnation's reads and sends, including prepared
exit permission. Missing, malformed and foreign heads merely withhold the reply.
A later head above the old floor cannot remove a proved restore refusal.
Neither can an older successful sync/adoption reply or a different partition
refusal overwrite it when that asynchronous work completes.

The Worker host retains the original head and capture until a strict commit
records the refusal through the existing `observe_store` operation. It drains
that proof before the next transaction and before close releases ownership;
a failed save or Worker restart keeps the proof for retry. An unavailable
page control snapshot cannot erase the request's capture; the host revalidates
identity when the Worker is available. Terminal publication
may have overtaken the original request while it waited: the host verifies the
same store, rebinds only the current watermark/send guards, and carries the
original floor/head into this refusal-only observation. It cannot grant progress,
adoption or sending authority. A changed store does not inherit the old proof.
As for ordinary observation, durable reopen refusal starts at the strict commit;
page-memory evidence before that boundary is not a physical-crash guarantee.

Exit preparation is a separate operation after an admission's committed reply.
Its failure preserves that success or known refusal (including `NOT_ADMIN`),
withdraws preparation permission and schedules bounded background recovery.
The Chromium regressions prove 100 → 90 → 101 with the Worker blocked, a new
pending admission, overtaking publication and offline reopen; failed proof-save
recovery; both preparation outcomes; and real Worker-emitted prediction tables
from a persisted predictable entry after the admission barrier clears.
The observer audit and negative controls are in
[SS round 7](../snapback4/reports/20260927-ss-sync-scale/ROUND7.md).

**2026-09-28 — SS round 8, provisional restore and failed initial claims.**
When page control is unavailable, a delayed cold reply fences the client
provisionally. The host reports its identity-validation outcome after strict
commit, retaining both the evidence and its completion callback across a failed
attempt or Worker restart. Recovering replacement B makes A's proof obsolete:
retire that provisional fence and resync B. This cannot clear another unresolved
proof or a confirmed refusal, including one established by ordinary observation.
The host keeps pending proofs and page fences by store, so evidence for a second
store cannot replace the first's custody. Confirmed same-store regressions keep
the existing sticky refusal and 100 → 90 → 101 behavior.

A failed quiescence probe during the initial store claim releases that claim
before rejecting. No device has opened under it; every later claimant still
performs the lifetime-lock and IndexedDB barrier before restoring. This differs
from a running owner's failed termination barrier, which still retains custody.
Both the default and Worker openers must retry on the primary store without an
abandoned lock or a forced alternate store. Chromium regressions also cover B's
restart and a failed validation commit, plus the complete Worker prediction
footprint and a count-only read after admission acknowledgement.

**2026-09-28 — SS round 9, failed close and adoption completion.** Close
always attempts Worker termination in `finally`, then releases the page claim
only after the lifetime-lock and IndexedDB barrier succeeds. A failed restore
save or an unexpected restore observation still rejects that close attempt,
but cannot abandon the primary lock. After release, later closes resolve
without retrying a closed owner. A failed termination barrier remains sticky
and retains the claim, as before. Failed close does not claim that its pending
restore proof became durable.

Chromium tests abort the strict restore save and substitute a non-refusal
observation; the next claimant must get `app` in both cases. A separate
generation-changing page is held first at observation, then in another case
at a successful adoption reply. Head 90 against the captured floor 100 must
still refuse the next action after either completion. The second case fails
when only the post-adoption restore guard is removed, with the earlier
observation guards intact. See
[SS round 9](../snapback4/reports/20260927-ss-sync-scale/ROUND9.md).

**2026-09-29 — HV heavy acquisition.** The built-in default and Worker hosts
use format 4, superseding the format-3 bucket procedure above for those hosts.
The public `indexedDbPersistence()` adapter still creates format 3 and can
read either layout. Custom persistence keeps its existing `Change[]` contract.
Physical IndexedDB version 3 fences actual format-3 clients (version 2).
The current public adapter still opens at version 2 on every operation: a
VersionError clears its cached packing before it retries at version 3. That
fences a migration completed before the call, but does not fence a migration
between a save's preliminary marker read and its write transaction (the
round-2 claim was too broad). The built-in adapter now reads the marker again
**inside the strict writing transaction, before issuing any writes**, and uses
that value for bucket routing. If format 4 replaced the preliminary layout,
it aborts the untouched transaction and retries the complete delta through the
page writer. Its directory revision and conditional authority checks still
apply; rejection or failure publishes nothing. Metadata-only writes remain
in their single strict transaction because they do not depend on row layout.
The Chromium regression holds the completed preliminary read's callback while
another built-in object migrates. Ordinary and conditional page saves, and the
Worker host's `commitIf` with a prepared-delta RPC fixture, write no buckets and
preserve point/load agreement; false predicates leave the whole old image.
Today's real Worker restricts conditional operations to metadata; the RPC fixture
supplies row changes to exercise the host's shared adapter directly.
Custom providers sharing a physical name must preserve exclusive ownership and
either re-read format inside each write transaction or atomically fence stale
format owners. A cached layout across an independently committed migration is
not a permitted provider behavior.
A format-3 store converts locally, without downloading its partition: one strict
transaction reads the bounded buckets and overflow entries, packs logical
`r`, `s` and `b` records into pages, and changes the marker. Metadata, outbox,
transfer acknowledgements, unfinished snapshots and confirmed prediction bases
retain their exact logical values. An abort leaves format 3 intact at physical
version 3; the updated client retries conversion. Old application/Worker bundles
must be replaced before opening it offline. Conversion is linear in the old
store and temporarily holds its logical images in the JS host.

A format-4 page holds at most 512 records or an estimated 256 KiB of key/value
bytes; a single larger existing record occupies its own page. Row payloads are
structured-cloned once, without a second JSON bucket string. Page-key records
form a compact directory. Its cached revision must equal the revision read in
the strict write transaction; a mismatch refuses and requires reload. Metadata,
page payloads, page keys and the next revision commit together. The cache advances
only on `oncomplete`. A proved complete page deletion avoids fetching its payload;
a partial deletion preserves every unrelated record. The authority predicate
and `commit()` stay in the same callback turn. Durability, claim ownership and
failed-save VM disposal remain as above; pages never split a device call into
several durability acknowledgements.

The memory device retains validated tagged JSON row images instead of keeping
one parsed field tree per row. Publication can share a canonical staged row's
substring only after comparing it with the whole canonical row encoding,
including nested values; old/noncanonical stages retain that canonical encoding
instead. This uses one temporary row serialization, not a whole-page copy, and
preserves sharing for canonical stages. The pricing scanner still recognizes
only canonical tagged spellings such as `{"Row":` and `{"Map":`; it is not exact
for every accepted JSON spelling. Canonical publication and restore keep
metered scans off that noncanonical path. Debug assertions at row-image load
and write/publication boundaries check the stored image against the canonical
serialization. Whitespace, escaped enum tags and map ordering are normalized
before these boundaries. Metered scans have
the same admission threshold for every accepted spelling, and refuse below it
before decoding. Reads decode only the requested rows, reserving decoder memory
before metered access. Index keys keep
their exact ordering and full id tie breaker while sharing a row's encoded id
suffix and row-id handle. Replacement collects and sorts keys into bounded index
pages, with one old row/index image for rollback. Indexes are complete before
prediction replay, coverage publication or a query can read them. Ordinary edits
retain transactional undo. Neither columns, indexes, rows nor horizons are removed.

The wasm bridge drains at most 512 changes and approximately 256 KiB per string
(one oversized record is indivisible); the host assembles the complete change
vector and performs one strict save. This bounds bridge scratch, not the entire
partition or JS process. Linear-memory high-water size is reported separately
from logical data and native allocator retention. The generated heavy regression
compares peak allocation to the old row/tree representation of the same keys and
rows, checks bridge size, and restores the complete offline partition. See the
[HV report](../snapback4/reports/20260929-hv-heavy-acquisition/REPORT.md) for paired
measurements, target misses, migration evidence and native memory limits.

**2026-09-30 — NA native acquisition.** Native replacement retains the same
page transactions, private staging and one final publication transaction. The
loader writes rows through the existing validation and cap counts, while appending the exact validated index keys to a connection-local
SQLite temporary heap. Before returning from replacement it installs every key
into the ordinary index B-tree in `(ti, k)` order. SQLite's external sorter can
spill; Rust does not accumulate the account's keys. This bounds the sorting
working set, not whole-device memory: publication retains delivery candidates
per row. Astra's round-0 review increased rows from 105,034 to 195,534 and
measured Rust peak allocations 21.48 → 37.99 MB and RSS 50,084 → 88,736 KiB.
The inherited row-count dependence remains. Grok measured about 700 MB of
scratch files and 1.07 GB total disk high-water for a 373.5 MB final store,
about 2.9× final size. Initial acquisition needs this extra disk headroom;
it is a workload observation, not a universal bound. Disk exhaustion rolls
back publication and permits retry after space is freed. The normal bounded page
cache, WAL and `synchronous=FULL` remain unchanged. The heap is dropped on both
success and failure; all failures propagate to the enclosing rollback. There
is no new durable format or recovery state, and no query or prediction may read
between clearing the partition and completing its indexes.

Rows, complete indexes, history, horizon boundaries, watermark, acquired state,
acknowledgements, delivery and prediction replay still commit together. A killed
owner leaves the previous published image or the complete replacement; a fresh
owner restarts private acquisition through the existing continuation fence.
Frequent native staging and metadata statements reuse the existing statement
cache, retaining one prepared insert across a row's index keys. Whole-partition
replacement suspends its connection's residency triggers, then computes the
same row and byte counters in one grouped SQLite scan before restoring those
triggers. Main or legacy temporary counters retain their namespace and prior
zero entries. Trigger changes and counters belong to the publication transaction;
failures roll them back with the rows. The process and Expo JSON protocol and web implementation are unchanged.
The crash model kills actual child processes at seeded SQLite execution cuts
and memory-host atomic-save cuts, checks row and coverage digests before restart,
then verifies successful restart and a second offline reopen. Its memory host
uses fsync/rename to model the web's indivisible save; it is not physical-browser
or power-loss evidence. Loader and index-install failure controls compare rows,
all physical index keys, cap counts and residency counters with ordinary writes.
Attribution, repeated envelope measurements and test outcomes are recorded in
[NA's report](../snapback4/reports/20260930-na-native-acquisition/REPORT.md).

#### 20.4.1 Proposed bounded word-index construction after row publication (HV round 1)

**Proposal for review, not implemented.** The round-1 phase measurements are in
[the report](../snapback4/reports/20260929-hv-heavy-acquisition/round1/REPORT.md).
Word-key validation/encoding, insertion into the bulk buffer and sorting are a
material share of heavy apply, but ordinary indexes, staging, row decoding and
delivery publication together cost more. Deferral moves work off the first
row-ready path; it does not remove work or make the entire account searchable
sooner. The current implementation still constructs every index synchronously.

**Publication and reads.** Keep the existing atomic replacement of rows,
ordinary indexes (including unique, cap, horizon and authorization indexes),
watermarks, acquisition boundaries, prediction bases, outbox and delivery debt.
That strict commit also records which word indexes require rebuilding, bound to
store identity, schema/index-definition hash and acquisition incarnation. There
is no interval in which new rows have old ordinary indexes or new coverage has
old rows. Indexes used for ordinary integrity or authorization cannot be deferred.
Required word-key label/byte admission remains a foreground obligation: do not
publish rows which the present key validator would refuse. A proposed cheap
path may prove a conservative upper bound from ASCII word-field byte lengths,
encoded non-word components and the full id suffix; it is allowed only when
that bound fits. Non-ASCII fields, oversized bounds and old-key shrink cases
keep exact current key generation/validation until a separately reviewed proof
covers them. Background construction may repeat that work, and its cost must
be counted. No server certification is substituted for a required device check.
This admission fast path is part of the proposal, not an implemented saving.
A query that depends on a pending word index must receive an incomplete verdict
*before* word expansion, including the empty-index and filled-page early exits.
Row coverage alone cannot certify it. Held/offline search may expose only known
matches with `complete: false`; it cannot claim absence or issue a continuation
that steps over unbuilt keys. A continuation from before the publication is
invalidated/restarted against its new index incarnation.

An ordinary online search may take its existing server path. The mixed search
coordinator must independently inspect retained-index readiness: a current server
answer cannot certify missing Left history. It either includes the incomplete
retained result and says `complete: false` without an unsafe continuation, or
waits for that local index. No app-owned branch, extra replication, new server
endpoint, or silent omission of retained matches is introduced. Predictions
whose reads require a pending word index remain queued for normal authoritative
execution; they never interpret an unbuilt index as an empty complete domain.
Ordinary-index-only reads and predictions keep their existing behavior. Index
readiness changes invalidate dependent watches through the ordinary device
notification path; fresh transport is independent of complete search coverage.

**Chunks and concurrent writes.** One device owner schedules work between calls;
no task runs outside its existing lifetime/authority fence. Proposed per-chunk
stops are 128 rows, 4,096 generated entries, 256 KiB of key scratch or a 4 ms
cooperative deadline, whichever comes first. These are experimental scheduling
limits, not raised query meters. A row is the smallest indivisible unit, admitted
under the existing row/key bounds; report its maximum overrun in validation.
Use a stable row-id traversal rather than an offset into changing rows. Every
chunk revalidates store, generation, acquisition and index definition. Updates,
deletes, expiry and scope revocation remove old word keys even during a build;
new/changed rows receive their current keys in the same row transaction. The
background cursor only advances over rows whose current version it indexed.
Rows inserted behind it are already indexed by their write. Replacement or
adoption cancels the previous build. A chunk that loses its fence publishes
nothing. Completion is one atomic transition after end-of-traversal and the
last write's index updates, never after merely scheduling the final chunk.
An indexing refusal leaves readiness false and preserves the normal online
path; it cannot advance a successful checkpoint or assert completion.

**Restore and crash recovery.** Persist the pending obligation with the rows in
the existing strict transaction. Browser indexes remain derived from durable row
images, so no durable cursor may authorize skipping work unless its corresponding
index pages were also durably saved. In the initial proposal, persist no browser
word keys: after process loss, discard all in-memory progress and rebuild from
the first row in bounded chunks. A previously persisted ready flag is not proof
that the new VM has any indexes; every open creates a new local build incarnation
and marks these indexes unavailable before serving search. Ordinary indexes must
still be rebuilt before ordinary row coverage is exposed. A failed strict save
discards the VM exactly as today; old durable rows and their old obligation win.
Native SQLite may persist word keys: each chunk must atomically commit keys and
its checkpoint under the same identity/version fence, and mark ready only with
the final keys. An older native reader that assumes complete indexes needs an
explicit persisted-format fence before partial indexes can be stored. The web's
older synchronous-rebuild reader is safe only because it rebuilds every key from
rows; neither host may trust an unknown readiness encoding. Format-3 row-store
upgrade, prediction-base restoration, revocation and restore-refusal rules remain.

**Expected cost and acceptance.** The numerical forecast follows the final
phase table in the round-1 report. From the measured 18.40 s default / 19.17 s
Worker total, forecast roughly **16.8–17.5 s / 17.6–18.3 s row-ready**, before
new scheduling overhead: the lower end needs the proposed bound proof to cover
most word-key admission; the upper keeps exact admission and moves only index
buffering/construction. Fully search-ready still pays the work: **at least about
18.4 / 19.2 s**, potentially about 0.6–0.7 s more when background construction
repeats foreground exact-key generation, plus scheduling overhead. These are
projections from instrumented phase shares, not measured deferred builds. Scheduler,
checkpoint and concurrent-write overhead are additional, unmeasured costs.
No under-8-second heavy-account claim follows from deferral alone. Acceptance
requires both stores and both browser hosts, interruption at every chunk/commit,
row edits on both sides of the cursor, insert/delete/revoke/expiry/adoption during
build, full offline reopening, empty/nonempty multi-term searches, mixed Left
history and continuation controls, with every absent-match claim checked against
a fully built reference index. Prove bounded scratch and fair progress under a
busy write stream. Any implementation must also fit the fixed wasm cap;
this round authorizes design and measurement only.

### 20.5 `upsert` predicts its insert when absence is provable (ruling 19; S20)

On a device, `upsert t[key] { … }` whose target the device does not hold
predicts the insert arm when two conditions both hold:
- **(a) The group is held with no horizon.** `t` is synced, and the key's
  group has no horizon, so the device holds every row of that group this
  viewer may read.
- **(b) The key decides readability.** The key determines readability, so no
  row hidden from this viewer can exist at that key. Examples: a read rule
  `public`, or `.col = viewer` with `col` in the key.

Otherwise the device queues without a row, as §8.7 (e) requires, and never
predicts `NOT_FOUND` or an insert for an unheld target. `check --residency`
and `why <op>` say which applies; the prediction card states the rule. Likes
and reactions keyed by `(post, viewer)` predict their first write offline.

**Read-through extension, QX (2026-09-30).** A key containing the immutable
parent reference decides the private child's readability through the existing
parent resolver. Public whole-table absence keeps its existing proof, including
complete view counts after parent expiry; an actual insert still validates the
parent capture and lifetime. A readable parent is not child coverage: prediction also needs the
child's whole acquired audience partition, no child horizon, matching captures,
and current (not retained, left, provisional or unfinished-rejoin) parent state.
A held parent may itself come from a horizon. Every secondary unique key and
cap prefix needs the same independent proof; expiring caps keep their restriction.
Unknown facts queue without a row. **QX round 1 correction:** holding a target
proves neither a secondary unique key nor a destination cap group. Every changed
non-null unique key and destination cap group needs complete readable coverage;
unchanged keys/groups need no new proof, and null unique keys do not collide.
Expiring cap moves still queue for server physical occupancy. These checks use
the separate device allowance and apply to updates as well as held upserts.
`check --residency` explains each constraint and calls blocked-insert upserts
`conditional updates`. The natural immutable `(parent, principal)` key and
`cap 50 by parent` preserve both first-write and replacement prediction. The server still judges the operation and a refusal
rolls back and replays pending work. Fixed capture reservations and the separate
device authorization allowance are unchanged. `insert … if absent` on a child
still queues; its explicit branch pattern remains on the prediction card only
for that case. No generated expression rewrite is introduced.

Membership keys may spell `.message.conversation` (or a third hop through an
inheriting parent) when they reproduce the parent's whole rule and satisfy its
immutable required-reference contract. They lower to the same read-through
captures, lifetime, audience and residency (LLP 3000.014 §2). QX's report is
`snapback4/reports/20260930-qx-first-instinct-forms/REPORT.md`.

**A refusal after an unproved insert (lane EX, 2026-10-08).** A plain `insert`
predicts without proving its supplied id, its secondary unique values or its cap
groups absent (ruling of 2026-10-08,
[ticket](../issues/closed/20261008-snapback4-device-predicts-insert-over-an-unheld-id.md)).
The server can then refuse that insert `E_RULE` while the device, carrying on over
its own predicted row, reaches a definite refusal in a later statement
(`E_CONSTRAINT` on a second insert of the id, `NOT_FOUND` on a second delete,
`E_OVERFLOW` on arithmetic). A device admission refusal is final for the client, so
the client reported a code the server never would
([ticket](../issues/closed/20261008-snapback4-device-refusal-after-an-unproved-prediction-differs-from-the-server.md)).
Now each authored plain device insert (not `if absent`, not an upsert's insert
arm, not the engine's timeline writes) records whether its id (unless minted for the call),
unique values and cap groups were proven absent by the same proof an upsert's
insert arm uses (`prove_upsert_insert`), run on the separate device allowance
(`device_work`); the proof's own unknown fact is discarded, so it never changes
the prediction's coverage, and an insert after an earlier unknown fact counts as
unproved. A minted id with no other unique key or cap needs no proof. A refusal after an unproved insert
becomes `E_PREDICT`: the write queues without a row and the server's verdict is the
one reported, including a refusal from final output pricing after evaluation.
A store failure or an `E_PREDICT` keeps its own message. A refusal
with no unproved insert before it stays final and local.

### 20.6 A read rule may name a service principal (ruling 20; S35)

A read rule may carry disjuncts `viewer = 'service:<name>'` beside its
audience rule. Services hold no partition, and the `service:` namespace is
reserved, so the sync audience is inferred from the rule with those
disjuncts removed; no device's partition changes. `check --residency` lists
the service grants. A second disjunct that is not a service principal is
still refused.

### 20.7 A public table may sync a subset to each device (ruling 21; S16)

A table whose read rule is `public` may declare a `sync` audience narrower
than the read rule (`sync to .followerId`, or an audience through another
table). A device then holds a subset of what its viewer may read. A read the
subset cannot decide is server-class, like a read past a horizon:
`complete: false` on the device, answered by the server online. A write to a
row inside the subset predicts as usual. `NOT-DOING.md` records the move in
the same change. The public-audience half of the exact-audience invariant
("never misses one it may") is given up deliberately for these tables; the
other half ("never holds a row it may not read") stands. The work lands
after wave 2.

### 20.8 The darwin binary is signed with Developer ID (ruling 22; S31)
